# SpecGuard Specifications

This directory is the **source of truth** for SpecGuard itself. Code is fluid; these specs, and the tests that prove the code conforms to them, are what stay put.

Specs describe *functionality that delivers user or business value*, not source files. One spec links to many code files, tests and docs.

## Layout

```
specs/
  system.md              # the master spec: problem, users, value, pillars, capability map
  capabilities/          # one spec per functional capability (~10)
    spec-authoring.md
    requirement-history.md
    traceability-and-drift.md
    conformance-testing.md
    agentic-verification.md
    documentation-api.md
    security-and-remediation.md
    workspaces.md
    integration-surfaces.md
    platform-foundation.md
  history/               # committed requirement history: prompts, approved plans, decisions
  README.md              # this file
```

Specs from the earlier per-file layout (`core/`, `pipelines/`, `cli/`, `adapters/`, `mcp/`, `extension/`, `plugins/`, `ci/`) still exist during the migration. They are archived under `_archive/v1/` when `specguard check` replaces the file-name-based `status` and `drift`. SpecGuard reads both formats.

## The v2 format

A spec starts with YAML frontmatter. Lists are block lists and every glob is quoted: a flow list such as `[a/{b,c}/**]` or an unquoted glob starting with `*` is invalid YAML, and the parser says so.

```markdown
---
id: spec-authoring            # must equal the file name
kind: capability              # system | capability | component | journey
title: Spec Authoring
parent: system                # a component's parent is a capability
value: One sentence: the user or business value this delivers.
status: active
sources:                      # code this spec owns; may overlap with other specs
  - "src/core/spec-parser.ts"
tests:
  - "tests/core/spec-parser.test.ts"
docs:
  - "README.md"
history:                      # ids of specs/history entries behind this spec
  - 2026-10-15-functional-specs-and-four-pillars
---

# Spec Authoring

## Problem & Value
## Users & Journeys
## Requirements
- [ ] A testable statement about behaviour <!-- claim: stable-claim-id -->
## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: name
**Steps:**
1. ...

**Expected Results:**
- ...
## Security & Data Considerations
## Interfaces
## Out of Scope
```

- `## Problem & Value` is required on capabilities and components. Agentic verification judges the running system against it.
- `## Requirements` replaces `## Acceptance Criteria`; bullets carry claim ids, `<!-- claim: id -->`, that tests cite with `@claim:<specKey>#<id>`.
- A claim's proof goes stale only when that claim's text or the spec's Problem & Value changes, or when the code it covers drifts. Editing another claim, a scenario, `sources` or `history` does not stale it.
- `system.md` is the one master spec (`kind: system`). Capabilities hang off it; a component refines a capability, for example its frontend and backend halves.
- A file may be owned by several specs. A source file owned by none is reported as unowned.

`specguard spec graph` prints the tree with owned-file counts and fails on rule violations: no or several system specs, an id that differs from the file name, an unknown parent, a capability without Problem & Value, a repeated claim id.

## Rules

- Write or update the spec **before** changing behaviour; the spec is the contract.
- Keep granularity at the capability level. If a spec only describes one file, merge it into the capability that file serves.
- Record why requirements changed in `specs/history/` (`specguard history add` once it exists; by hand until then).

# Agentic Verification

## Problem & Value
Unit and integration tests show that individual pieces behave as coded. They do not show that the finished, running application lets a user accomplish what the spec promised, or that it delivers the business value the spec exists for. End-to-end suites close part of that gap but are expensive to write and brittle to maintain, and they only check what someone thought to script.

Agentic verification points an LLM-driven browser agent at the running application. It looks at the page the way a user would (a screenshot plus the accessibility tree), plans the few interactions needed to check each acceptance criterion, performs them under strict guardrails, and returns an evidence-backed verdict per criterion. Because it works from the spec's own words, it needs no scripted selectors, and it can never delete data or send messages on its own.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard validate --spec <key> --url http://localhost:3000` after a change to see which acceptance criteria the live page fails, with screenshots as evidence.
- A QA lead runs `specguard validate --all` against staging with `--allow-outbound` to exercise flows that send notifications, while deletion stays blocked.
- A security-minded engineer defines an auth profile per role (for example admin and member) so each spec is verified as the right kind of user and logins never mix.
- A reviewer reads `.specguard/reports/` to see UX, accessibility and functional issues the agent noticed beyond the stated criteria.
- A CI job reads the exit code and `.specguard/validation-history.json` to track whether verdicts are improving over time.
- a product owner reads a per-capability judgement of whether the observed behaviour actually delivers the stated value.

## Requirements
- [ ] Validation targets specs that declare a `url:`, accepts a single spec, all specs or one app, resolves relative URLs against a base URL override, and skips with a message a spec that has no URL. <!-- claim: validate-targets -->
- [ ] For each spec the agent perceives the page through a screenshot and an accessibility snapshot, plans a short list of atomic browser actions from the acceptance criteria, performs them and then judges each criterion against the resulting state. <!-- claim: perceive-plan-act-verify -->
- [ ] Every acceptance criterion receives exactly one verdict from PASS, FAIL, BLOCKED or INCONCLUSIVE, a FAIL cites its evidence, and a failed LLM call or unavailable evidence yields INCONCLUSIVE rather than a pass. <!-- claim: criterion-verdicts -->
- [ ] The command exits with the validation-failed code (2) when any criterion or login fails and 0 otherwise, so skipped specs and blocked actions alone do not fail a run. <!-- claim: validate-exit-code -->
- [ ] Screenshots and page evidence are stored per spec under `.specguard/evidence/`, and every run appends an entry with its verdicts and overall result to `.specguard/validation-history.json`. <!-- claim: evidence-and-history -->
- [ ] An optional review step, skipped with `--no-review` or for specs with no UI sections, produces a typed issue report of functional, UX, accessibility and visual problems under `.specguard/reports/`. <!-- claim: review-issue-report -->
- [ ] Planned actions are classified as safe, destructive or outbound by deterministic whole-word keyword rules, with the real control's role and accessible name taking precedence over the planner's description when the target is known. <!-- claim: action-classification -->
- [ ] Destructive and outbound actions are blocked before execution and surfaced as BLOCKED verdicts with the reason, deny and allow rules in configuration override the built-in lists, and outbound actions run only when explicitly allowed while destructive ones are never allowed. <!-- claim: guardrail-blocking -->
- [ ] Authentication profiles support form login, saved browser state, header and token credentials, and a project-supplied script, and a login succeeds when a configured success URL or selector is reached, or otherwise when the browser leaves the login page. <!-- claim: auth-strategies -->
- [ ] A login failure, unknown profile or missing credential environment variable is reported as a clear authentication failure for the affected specs, and a successful login is cached so each profile logs in once per run. <!-- claim: auth-failures-and-cache -->
- [ ] Each auth profile runs in its own browser context and a spec without a profile runs in an anonymous context that is never logged in. <!-- claim: one-context-per-profile -->
- [ ] Credentials are read only from environment variables and never appear in config output, evidence, history, logs or LLM prompts, and error text derived from a login is redacted. <!-- claim: credentials-never-leak -->
- [ ] Page text, accessibility text and console errors pass through the redactor before reaching the LLM, and no screenshot is sent when images are disallowed in configuration. <!-- claim: redact-before-llm -->
- [ ] The browser is headless unless configured or `--headed` is passed, runs locally or in Docker as configured, and a missing Playwright installation produces an error with install instructions. <!-- claim: browser-lifecycle -->
- [ ] Evidence, saved login state and report directories are created with a `.gitignore` that excludes their contents. <!-- claim: evidence-gitignored -->
- [ ] validation goals are built per capability from its Users & Journeys and Scenarios, so the agent walks real user journeys instead of isolated criteria. <!-- claim: capability-goals -->
- [ ] the judge also receives the capability's Problem & Value and returns a capability-level judgement of whether the observed behaviour delivers the stated value, reporting gaps as findings. <!-- claim: value-judgement -->
- [ ] verdicts are written into the proof ledger with evidence marked as agentic, so `check` treats browser verification as first-class proof alongside test results. <!-- claim: ledger-proof -->
- [ ] `verify` takes every v2 capability when given a base URL, even one with no `url:` of its own, and walks up to `validate.maxRounds` (default 3) plan-act rounds so one run can cross pages; the page is not reloaded between rounds <!-- claim: verify-walks-journeys -->
- [ ] Only PASS and FAIL verdicts are written as proof; BLOCKED and INCONCLUSIVE never overwrite a proof a test run earned, and a verdict is matched to a requirement by its id (exact, or followed by a delimiter) or its exact text, never by substring <!-- claim: verify-proof-matching -->
- [ ] A capability whose value is judged NO fails the verification even when every requirement passes, and the judgement with its gaps is written to `.specguard/reports/verify-<spec>.json` <!-- claim: verify-value-fails -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: All criteria pass
**Steps:**
1. A spec declares `url:` for a running app.
2. A developer runs `specguard validate --spec <key>`.

**Expected Results:**
- Each criterion gets a PASS verdict.
- A history entry is appended and the command exits 0.

### Scenario 2: A criterion fails with evidence
**Steps:**
1. The page does not show a confirmation the spec requires.
2. `specguard validate --spec <key>` runs.

**Expected Results:**
- The criterion is FAIL and the message cites a screenshot path under `.specguard/evidence/`.
- The command exits with code 2.

### Scenario 3: A destructive action is planned
**Steps:**
1. The planner proposes clicking a control named "Delete account" to check a criterion.
2. Guardrails classify the target by its accessible name.

**Expected Results:**
- The action is not executed and a `[blocked]` line is printed.
- The affected criterion is BLOCKED, not PASS or FAIL.
- The same holds with `--allow-outbound`, because destructive actions are never allowed.

### Scenario 4: Role-specific verification
**Steps:**
1. Two specs name different auth profiles, `admin` and `member`, with credentials in environment variables.
2. `specguard validate --all` runs.

**Expected Results:**
- Each profile logs in once, in its own browser context.
- A spec with no profile runs anonymously.
- If a credential variable is unset, the affected specs fail with a missing-variable message that contains no credential value.

### Scenario 5: Spec without a URL
**Steps:**
1. A spec has no `url:` and no base URL is provided.
2. `specguard validate --all` runs.

**Expected Results:**
- The spec is skipped with a reason and does not affect the exit code.

### Scenario 6: value-level judgement
**Steps:**
1. A capability spec lists user journeys and a Problem & Value statement.
2. The planned validation walks each journey.

**Expected Results:**
- A capability-level judgement states whether the observed behaviour delivers the stated value.
- Gaps appear as findings and verdicts are recorded in the proof ledger as agentic evidence.

## Security & Data Considerations
The agent acts on a live application, so safety rests on layered controls: deterministic guardrails block destructive and outbound actions before they run, credentials come only from environment variables and are redacted from every string that could be logged or sent, and each login lives in an isolated browser context. Page text, accessibility text and console errors are redacted before they reach the LLM, and screenshots are sent only when the configuration allows images. Evidence screenshots can contain personal data, so evidence and saved login state are git-ignored and should be treated as confidential. Verification should target staging or local environments with test accounts, not production data.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard validate [--spec <key>] [--all] [--url <base>] [--app <name>] [--no-review] [--headed] [--allow-outbound]`. With neither `--spec` nor `--all` the command fails with a usage error.
- MCP tool: `specguard_validate`.
- Config: `auth.profiles[]` (name, strategy, loginUrl, usernameEnvVar, passwordEnvVar, successUrl, successSelector, storageStatePath, scriptPath), `validate.headless`, `validate.guardrails.{allow,deny,allowOutbound}`, `validate.redaction`, `llm.allowImages`, `runners.playwright`.
- Files: `.specguard/evidence/<spec-key>/`, `.specguard/auth/<profile>.json`, `.specguard/reports/validate-<spec-key>.json`, `.specguard/validation-history.json`.
- Exit codes: 0 all passed or skipped, 2 any criterion or login failed, 1 usage or internal error.

## Out of Scope
- Generating or running scripted tests (see conformance-testing).
- Load, performance or visual-regression testing.
- Bypassing guardrails or running destructive actions against any environment.
- Interactive second-factor logins; use saved state, tokens or a script instead.

# Conformance Testing

## Problem & Value
A spec is only a claim until something shows the code honours it. Tests written by hand drift from the spec, tests written by an LLM may assert nothing meaningful, and a green run yesterday says little about the code changed today. Reviewers cannot tell which requirements are actually exercised, which merely have a test file with a similar name, and which proofs have silently expired.

Conformance testing turns specs into tests, runs the project's own test suite through whatever runner it uses, and reduces the results to one verdict per claim in a single proof ledger. A proof records exactly what it was based on (the claim text, the source files, the dependencies), so it goes stale the moment any of those change. Failing tests are triaged into "the test is wrong" and "the application is wrong", and only the first is ever repaired automatically.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard generate --spec <key>` to turn a spec's scenarios into a test file whose titles carry claim tags.
- A CI job runs the project's tests, then `specguard results ingest report.json` to record a verdict for every tagged claim without any LLM call.
- A developer runs `specguard heal` after a refactor to learn which failing tests are stale and have them rewritten, and which failures are real application bugs.
- A reviewer runs `specguard proof status` to see which claims are failed or stale before approving a release.
- An external system (a QA service, a manual test tool) posts a verdicts file with `specguard proof ingest` so its evidence appears next to the rest.
- A polyglot team points the same flow at pytest, go test, cargo test or Maven Surefire output without changing how claims are tagged.

## Requirements
- [ ] Generation turns every scenario of a spec into one test block titled with the scenario name, importing the module the spec declares, for a single spec or all specs and optionally limited to one app. <!-- claim: generate-per-scenario -->
- [ ] Generation supports unit, integration and end-to-end test types, uses the owning app's framework unless overridden, and uses a browser framework for end-to-end tests in TypeScript. <!-- claim: generate-test-types -->
- [ ] When a spec has claims, the generation prompt lists each claim with its exact tag and requires it in the verifying test's title, and generation warns about every claim whose tag is missing from the output while still writing the file. <!-- claim: generate-claim-tags -->
- [ ] Generation never overwrites an existing test file unless forced, strips stray Markdown fences from LLM output, and records an LLM failure for one spec without stopping the others. <!-- claim: generate-safe-writes -->
- [ ] A claim tag is recognised in the forms `@claim:<spec>#<id>`, `[claim: <spec>#<id>]` and `[claims: a#b, c#d]`, in titles, tags and annotations, with an optional repository prefix, and all consumers read tags through the same logic. <!-- claim: claim-tag-forms -->
- [ ] Tests are run through a runner adapter for vitest, jest, playwright, pytest, any JUnit-producing runner, go and cargo, and results are always read from the reporter's output file, never scraped from stdout. <!-- claim: runner-adapters -->
- [ ] Adapters inject the reporter flags the runner needs (with a single separator for npm scripts), run the command verbatim when a results file is configured, pass a test selection as file arguments, merge a results glob, kill a run that exceeds its timeout, and can run inside a Docker sandbox with the repository mounted, where a missing Docker or image is a clear failure that never falls back to the host. <!-- claim: runner-invocation -->
- [ ] Reporter output of every supported format is normalised into one result shape covering passes, failures and skips, the format can be auto-detected, and unparseable input is a named error rather than an empty list. <!-- claim: normalised-results -->
- [ ] A claim's verdict is failed when any tagged test fails, proven when at least one passes and none fail, and unexercised otherwise, with counts of exercised tests and counterexamples. <!-- claim: claim-verdict-rule -->
- [ ] The proof ledger stores proven, failed, unexercised and error verdicts; stale is computed and never stored, and unproven means the ledger has no row for the claim. <!-- claim: ledger-verdict-states -->
- [ ] A proof is stale when the spec (or, for v2 specs, the claim) hash changed, when a source file recorded at ingest changed on disk, or when the repository's dependency fingerprint changed; a file that vanished from the registry alone does not make it stale. <!-- claim: stale-rule -->
- [ ] Each stored row records the claim hash, the source file hashes taken from the spec's declared sources, the dependency fingerprint, the run id, the git revision and the evidence path, so editing one source file stales exactly the claims of the specs that declare it. <!-- claim: ledger-records-basis -->
- [ ] Ingesting verdicts rejects a file without a run id or verdicts, fails and does not store a verdict for an unparseable reference, missing spec or unknown claim, and lets a later ingest replace an earlier row. <!-- claim: ingest-validation -->
- [ ] `results ingest` merges several report files before aggregating, detects or accepts an explicit format, accepts a run id, records a repo-relative evidence path, and exits 2 when any claim failed or a file could not be parsed. <!-- claim: results-ingest -->
- [ ] A partial ingest only writes verdicts for claims present in the results, while the sweep option stores unexercised for absent claims only on a declared full run and never downgrades a still-matching proven claim. <!-- claim: partial-and-sweep -->
- [ ] `proof ingest` and `results ingest` share one code path, write identical rows for identical verdicts, and use a ledger path from `--ledger`, then `paths.proofLedger`, then `.specguard/proofs.json`, kept portable with repo-relative keys. <!-- claim: shared-ingest-and-ledger-path -->
- [ ] Each proof row records its provenance: `origin` (`ci` on a GitHub Actions or other CI run, `local` otherwise, `server` for a server-side run), repository, branch, CI actor (never a developer's git identity) and the claim-hash version in force; ledger writes go through one store interface (a file by default) that serialises concurrent updates so none is lost, and a ledger written by a newer SpecGuard is refused rather than read as empty and overwritten <!-- claim: proof-provenance -->
- [ ] `proof status` lists failed and stale claims and exits 2 when any exist, while `status` shows proof counts without changing its exit code and `drift` reports each stale proof. <!-- claim: proof-reporting -->
- [ ] Healing runs one job per distinct test command, classifies each failing test as a test bug or an application bug, rewrites only test code and re-runs up to the retry budget, and never modifies application source. <!-- claim: heal-classifies-failures -->
- [ ] Healing treats a missing or unparseable report as a failure even when the runner exited 0 unless told to be lenient, exits 7 while any test remains broken including application bugs, and with classify-only never writes or re-runs. <!-- claim: heal-exit-and-safety -->
- [ ] Framework detection recognises common web, API and CLI frameworks from the repository's manifests, falls back to a generic profile and honours an explicit entry-point override. <!-- claim: framework-profiles -->
- [ ] `test run` runs each configured app's tests through its runner adapter, reads the report from the file the runner writes, and ingests the verdicts into the proof ledger in one step, so tests run locally and results produced by CI land in the same ledger <!-- claim: test-run-ingests -->
- [ ] `test run` exits non-zero when a suite fails, when a runner produces no readable report, or when a tagged claim fails, even if no failing test carries a claim tag <!-- claim: test-run-fails-honestly -->
- [ ] A proof records what produced it: a test run leaves `evidence` unset and an agentic browser run records `agentic` <!-- claim: proof-evidence-kind -->
- [ ] `test generate`, `test run` and `test heal` group the test commands; the older `generate` and `heal` names keep working <!-- claim: test-command-group -->
- [ ] After a consolidation, results that still carry old claim tags are accepted for one release through `.specguard/claim-migration.json` and recorded under the new claim refs <!-- claim: old-claim-tags-accepted -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Spec to tagged tests
**Steps:**
1. A capability spec has two claims and three scenarios.
2. A developer runs `specguard generate --spec <key> --type unit`.

**Expected Results:**
- One test file is written with one test per scenario.
- Titles of the tests that verify the claims include the exact `@claim:` tags.
- Running again without `--force` skips the file and makes no LLM call.

### Scenario 2: CI records proof from a normal test run
**Steps:**
1. CI runs the suite with a JSON or JUnit reporter.
2. CI runs `specguard results ingest report.json --run-id build-42`.

**Expected Results:**
- Each tagged claim gets `proven`, `failed` or `unexercised` according to its tests.
- Each row carries the source hashes and dependency fingerprint of that moment.
- The command exits 2 if any claim failed and 0 otherwise.

### Scenario 3: A source edit invalidates only the right proofs
**Steps:**
1. Proofs exist for claims in two specs; only the first declares `src/a.ts`.
2. A developer edits `src/a.ts`.
3. `specguard proof status` runs.

**Expected Results:**
- Claims of the first spec are reported stale.
- Claims of the second spec remain proven.
- The command exits 2 because stale proofs exist.

### Scenario 4: Heal separates test bugs from application bugs
**Steps:**
1. After a refactor two tests fail: one asserts an old label, one catches a real regression.
2. A developer runs `specguard heal`.

**Expected Results:**
- The stale assertion is classified as a test bug, rewritten and the suite re-run.
- The regression is reported as an application bug with a reason and no source is changed.
- The command exits 7 because the suite is still red.

### Scenario 5: A broken report is not a pass
**Steps:**
1. The test command exits 0 but writes no parseable results file.
2. A developer runs `specguard heal`.

**Expected Results:**
- The run is reported as a failure with exit code 7.
- With `--lenient` the same situation is treated as passing.

### Scenario 6: External evidence is submitted
**Steps:**
1. A QA service writes a verdicts file with a run id and verdicts for claim references.
2. It runs `specguard proof ingest verdicts.json`.

**Expected Results:**
- Valid claims are stored, replacing earlier rows for the same claim.
- A reference to a claim with no anchor in its spec is reported as failed and not stored.

### Scenario 7: A polyglot suite
**Steps:**
1. A Python service configures `test: { command: "pytest" }`.
2. `heal` or `results ingest` runs against the generated JUnit XML.

**Expected Results:**
- Pytest runs with a JUnit reporter flag and results are read from the file.
- Claim tags in test names or properties map to claims exactly as for other runners.

## Security & Data Considerations
Test commands come from the repository's own configuration and run with the developer's or CI's privileges; the Docker sandbox option isolates them when the code is not trusted. Heal and generate send test code, spec text and failure messages to the LLM and are subject to configured redaction, and heal only ever writes test files. Verdict files from external systems are untrusted input: they are schema-checked, every claim reference must resolve to an anchored claim, and unknown references are rejected rather than stored. The ledger holds hashes, counts and relative paths, never secrets, and its keys are repo-relative so it is portable. Evidence paths must stay inside the repository.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard generate [--spec <key>] [--all] [--app <name>] [--framework <name>] [--force] [--type unit|integration|e2e]`; `specguard heal [--spec] [--all] [--app] [--max-retries <n>] [--classify-only] [--lenient]`; `specguard results ingest <file...> [--format auto|vitest|jest|playwright|junit|pytest|go|cargo] [--run-id <id>] [--unexercised|--sweep] [--full-run] [--ledger <file>]`; `specguard proof ingest <verdicts> [--ledger <file>]`; `specguard proof status [--ledger <file>]`.
- MCP tools: `specguard_generate`, `specguard_heal`, `specguard_results_ingest`, `specguard_proof_ingest`, `specguard_proof_status`.
- Files: `.specguard/proofs.json` (or `paths.proofLedger`, workspace root when a workspace file exists); per-app config `test: { command, cwd, reporter, resultsFile, timeoutMs, image }`; `heal.maxRetries`, `heal.testCommand`.
- Claim tag: `@claim:<specKey>#<claimId>`.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 2 failed or stale claims or unparseable results, 7 heal failed.

## Out of Scope
- Replacing the project's test runner or CI system.
- Judging the running system in a browser (see agentic-verification).
- Detecting drift between source and specs (see traceability-and-drift).
- Repairing application source code (see security-and-remediation for planned fixes).

# Documentation and API

## Problem & Value
Documentation goes stale the moment code changes, and hand-written docs rarely keep up. A single static document also cannot serve everyone: end users want to know what the system does, developers want to know where and how, and AI agents want compact, structured context they can load cheaply. Teams end up with docs that are wrong, or with several copies written for different readers that disagree.

Because the specs are kept current and traceable to code and tests, they are the right source for documentation. This capability rewrites specs into readable docs with an LLM, keeps marked sections of the repository's front-door files in sync, and exposes audit views such as the traceability matrix. The main planned direction is a read-only API and small web UI, `specguard serve`, that generates user, developer and agent documentation on demand from the specs with a fast model, so what a reader sees always reflects the current specs.

## Users & Journeys
- A product owner runs `specguard docs --all` to produce user-facing pages under `docs/user/`, each with a category and reading order for a docs site.
- A maintainer runs `specguard docs` and finds the architecture, commands and pipeline sections of `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md` refreshed without touching hand-written text.
- An auditor opens the traceability matrix and audit data as documents to review how requirements map to tests and docs.
- a viewer application calls `GET /api/v1/docs/user/<capability>` and renders current, user-level documentation without any build step.
- a coding agent calls `GET /api/v1/docs/agent/system` to load a compact structured briefing before changing code.
- a developer opens the bundled web UI at `http://localhost:<port>/` to browse capabilities, their trace and their history.

## Requirements
- [ ] `docs` rewrites a single spec, all specs or one app's specs into user-facing Markdown pages under `docs/user/` (or a chosen output directory), mirroring the spec's relative path. <!-- claim: docs-per-spec -->
- [ ] Internal-only content (the metadata comment, scenarios and security notes) is removed before the LLM sees the spec, and the rewrite must stay accurate to the supplied spec without inventing features. <!-- claim: docs-strip-internal -->
- [ ] Each generated page starts with frontmatter holding a title, sidebar label, description, category, reading order and a flag marking it as generated. <!-- claim: docs-frontmatter -->
- [ ] Generated docs are regenerable artifacts that overwrite existing files, an LLM failure on one spec is recorded and does not stop the others, and the command fails only if every attempted spec failed. <!-- claim: docs-failure-isolation -->
- [ ] After per-spec docs are generated, marked sections of `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` (only if it exists) and `AGENTS.md` are replaced between start and end markers, appended when absent, and hand-written content outside the markers is never altered. <!-- claim: root-doc-sync-sentinels -->
- [ ] `AGENTS.md` is created from a template when missing and only its marked sections are updated when present, and a failure to generate the section text logs the error and writes nothing. <!-- claim: root-doc-sync-safe -->
- [ ] LLM credentials never appear in any generated page or synchronised section. <!-- claim: docs-no-secrets -->
- [ ] The traceability matrix and audit data produced by the audit commands are plain JSON or CSV files under `.specguard/` that viewers and auditors can load as documents. <!-- claim: audit-data-as-documents -->
- [ ] `specguard serve` starts a read-only HTTP server on `node:http` bound to localhost under `/api/v1`, with no endpoint that writes, runs a pipeline or executes code; a malformed request target or percent-encoding is answered with 400 and never stops the server. <!-- claim: serve-readonly -->
- [ ] `GET /system`, `/capabilities`, `/capabilities/:id` and `/capabilities/:id/history` return the system spec, the capability list with their value statements, one capability's parsed content, and its requirement history. <!-- claim: spec-endpoints -->
- [ ] `GET /trace`, `/audit` and `/security/plans` return the traceability data, the audit views and the stored remediation plans in their existing stable JSON shapes. <!-- claim: audit-endpoints -->
- [ ] `GET /docs/:audience/:id` and `/docs/:audience/system` return generated documentation for the audience `user`, `dev` or `agent`, and an unknown audience or capability returns a clear 400 or 404 error. <!-- claim: docs-endpoints -->
- [ ] the user audience omits claims and internals, the dev audience adds sources, interfaces and tests, and the agent audience is a compact structured form that can be parsed without reading prose. <!-- claim: audience-shapes -->
- [ ] documentation is generated on demand with the fast model tier, never in the background, and responses are complete documents rather than streams. <!-- claim: fast-tier-on-demand -->
- [ ] generated documents are cached (behind a cache interface, files by default) by spec content hash, audience, prompt version, model and the enabled plugin renderers, so an unchanged spec is served from cache and an edited spec, a changed prompt version or a different model regenerates it. <!-- claim: cache-key -->
- [ ] concurrent requests for the same uncached document share one LLM call (single-flight), different documents generate concurrently, and each generation runs in its own LLM scope with its own budget (a spent budget fails that request with a clear error and never affects or resets another) and with the requester's name sent to the model gateway for spend attribution. <!-- claim: single-flight-budget -->
- [ ] a small static web UI served at `/` lets a person browse the system, capabilities, trace and generated docs using only the API. <!-- claim: static-ui -->
- [ ] served documents and data are redacted so credentials and secret values from specs, config or history never leave the server. <!-- claim: served-redaction -->
- [ ] On a loopback address the server rejects any request whose Host header is not a local name (blocking DNS-rebinding reads from a hostile page), answers with `nosniff`, no-store and a content security policy on the UI, and sends cross-origin headers only when `--cors` names an origin <!-- claim: serve-host-guard -->
- [ ] The web UI escapes all HTML in model-written markdown and links only http(s), site-relative and anchor URLs, so generated docs cannot inject script <!-- claim: ui-escapes-markdown -->
- [ ] When the model is unavailable the user and dev audiences are rendered directly from the spec with a warning and are not cached, so the next request tries the model again; a spent LLM budget is reported as HTTP 429 instead <!-- claim: docs-model-fallback -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Generate user docs
**Steps:**
1. A repository has capability specs.
2. A developer runs `specguard docs --all`.

**Expected Results:**
- One Markdown page per spec is written under `docs/user/`.
- Each page has frontmatter with title, category, order and `generated: true`.
- Scenarios and security notes do not appear in the page.

### Scenario 2: Root docs stay in sync without losing hand-written text
**Steps:**
1. `README.md` has hand-written intro text and an existing marked architecture section.
2. `specguard docs --all` runs.

**Expected Results:**
- The marked section is replaced exactly once with new text.
- The hand-written text is unchanged.
- If section text generation fails, no root file is modified and the run continues.

### Scenario 3: One spec fails to document
**Steps:**
1. The LLM errors for one of five specs.
2. `specguard docs --all` runs.

**Expected Results:**
- The failure is recorded and the other four pages are written.
- The command exits non-zero only if all five failed.

### Scenario 4: on-demand user docs
**Steps:**
1. A viewer requests `GET /api/v1/docs/user/traceability-and-drift`.
2. Another viewer requests the same document at the same moment.

**Expected Results:**
- One fast-model call is made and both receive the same non-streamed document without claims or internals.
- A repeat request is served from cache until the spec text or prompt version changes.

### Scenario 5: agent briefing
**Steps:**
1. An agent requests `GET /api/v1/docs/agent/system`.

**Expected Results:**
- The response is a compact structured document listing capabilities, their value and their interfaces.
- An unknown audience returns a clear client error.

### Scenario 6: browsing in the web UI
**Steps:**
1. A developer runs `specguard serve` and opens `http://localhost:<port>/`.

**Expected Results:**
- The UI lists capabilities and shows each one's trace, history and generated docs, all read from `/api/v1`.
- The server is reachable only from the local machine.

## Security & Data Considerations
Documentation generation sends spec text to the LLM, so it passes through the configured redaction, and only non-internal sections are sent for user docs. Credential values must not be written into docs or root-file sections. Marked-section replacement touches only the text between markers so hand-written content cannot be overwritten. The planned server is read-only, binds to localhost by default and has no endpoint that mutates state or runs commands. Its LLM spend is bounded per request, and cached documents are keyed by content hash so stale or tampered text is never served as current. Exposing the server beyond localhost requires an explicit choice and is not covered by this spec.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard docs [--spec <key>] [--all] [--out <path>] [--app <name>]`, printing a summary line `docs: <N> created, <N> skipped, <N> failed`.
- MCP tool: `specguard_docs` (and `specguard_matrix` for the matrix document).
- Files: `docs/user/<feature>.md` with frontmatter (`title`, `sidebar_label`, `description`, `category`, `order`, `generated`); marked sections `<!-- specguard:<key>:start -->` and `<!-- specguard:<key>:end -->` in `README.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`; `.specguard/traceability.json` and audit data.
- CLI: `specguard serve [--port <n>] [--host <addr>] [--cors <origin>]`.
- HTTP (GET only, under `/api/v1`): `/system`, `/capabilities`, `/capabilities/:id`, `/capabilities/:id/history`, `/trace`, `/audit`, `/docs/:audience/:id`, `/docs/:audience/system`, `/security/plans`; static UI at `/`.
- Config: the fast model tier from `llm.models.fast`, and a per-request budget.
- Exit codes: 0 success, non-zero when every attempted document failed.

## Out of Scope
- Hosting a general public documentation site; the API is for viewers to render from.
- Authentication and multi-user access control for the planned server.
- Streaming responses and editing documents through the API.
- Producing the traceability matrix itself (see traceability-and-drift).

# Integration Surfaces - CLI, Agents, CI, IDE and Plugins

## Problem & Value
A spec-driven tool is only useful if it fits into how work is actually done. Developers live in a terminal, coding agents in a harness such as an agent CLI or an editor, release managers in CI, and reviewers in an IDE. If each of those needed different setup, behaved differently, or silently changed the user's own configuration, SpecGuard would not be adopted or trusted. Teams also have platform-specific conventions (feature catalogs, test-management ids, lint tools) that must not be hard-wired into the core.

This capability is the set of surfaces through which people, agents and systems drive SpecGuard: one command line with stable exit codes and machine-readable output, an `init` that sets a project up and wires agents in without clobbering anything, an MCP server that exposes the same operations to agents, a GitHub Action that turns checks into pass or fail gates, a VS Code extension with a dashboard, and a plugin system for optional, generalised features such as the feature catalog, code quality and git helpers.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard init` in a repo and gets a config, a specs directory and agent files; running it again changes nothing.
- A coding agent starts a session, finds the MCP server and the CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md instructions that init wrote, and calls tools such as `specguard_status` and `specguard_drift` after each change.
- A release manager adds the GitHub Action with `fail-on: drift,proof-failed` so a pull request fails on the right conditions, and schedules `mode: remediate` for dependency fixes.
- A reviewer opens the VS Code dashboard to see coverage, last pipeline runs and agent activity without leaving the editor.
- A platform team enables `feature-catalog` by name and describes its catalog layout, id scheme and result sources in `featureState` config; an unknown plugin name is reported, not ignored.
- A team lead runs `specguard features --state` to see, per catalogued feature, which of UI, API and MCP are built, passing or proven and whether an agent may run on it.
- A developer runs `specguard quality` and `specguard commit` to lint and commit only SpecGuard-generated files.

## Requirements
- [ ] The `specguard` command routes each subcommand to its pipeline and prints help for every subcommand; `--version` prints the package version and `--version --json` prints one JSON line with name, version and Node version; an unknown subcommand exits non-zero with a usage hint; global options `--config <path>` (a file, a directory, or a path containing `/.specguard/`), `--json` (machine-readable result with the exit code, human output suppressed) and `--record` reach every command <!-- claim: cli-routing-and-flags -->
- [ ] Exit codes are typed and stable (0 success, 1 internal or usage error, 2 validation failed, 3 drift, 4 missing specs, 5 security issues, 7 heal failed, 8 LLM budget exceeded); a SpecGuard error prints its message to stderr and exits with its own code, an unexpected error exits 1, and a refused LLM call for budget forces exit 8; a missing config exits 1 with the instruction to run `specguard init`, and `.specguard/.env` variables are loaded before commands run without overwriting existing environment variables <!-- claim: exit-codes-and-env -->
- [ ] `init` creates `.specguard/config.json`, `specs/README.md` and a `.specguard/.env` containing only a placeholder key, detects the language and test framework (Playwright forced by `--with-playwright`), never overwrites existing files and reports created and skipped paths; it adds a managed git-ignore block for generated state and prints the untrack command when git already tracks such files <!-- claim: init-bootstrap -->
- [ ] `init` and `scaffold` generate agent-harness files for Claude, Cursor or both: a CLAUDE.md with managed sections, per-harness skill files, a goal command and AGENTS.md, all marked as SpecGuard-managed and using language-specific commands; a marked file is refreshed, an unmarked hand-written file is left alone, and content outside managed sections is preserved <!-- claim: harness-files -->
- [ ] Setup merges an MCP server entry and a post-edit status hook into the agent's settings without removing unrelated keys (malformed existing JSON is reported and left unchanged); the generated commands use a resolved runner (`--runner node|npx|path`, otherwise `SPECGUARD_CLI`, a local binary, a global binary, then `npx -p specguard-ai specguard`); an entry written in an older broken form is repaired, and any other differing existing entry is never rewritten silently: a diff is printed and the file left alone unless `--update-hooks` is given <!-- claim: agent-wiring-and-runner -->
- [ ] The MCP server runs over stdio, registers one tool per core command plus `read_spec` and `write_spec` (the pre-0.2 names only with `SPECGUARD_MCP_LEGACY=1`), calls the same pipeline functions as the CLI with an optional `cwd`, returns a text summary (counts, messages, items, raw result) and returns an error result instead of throwing; importing the module does not start the transport <!-- claim: mcp-tools-parity -->
- [ ] Every MCP tool call appends a running entry and then a pass, fail or error entry with duration to `.specguard/activity-log.json`, which is bounded to the latest 200 entries once it exceeds 1 MB, recovers from invalid JSON and never throws; `read_spec` needs a spec key or path; MCP tools never perform effects outside the machine (remediate is scan-only and dry-run only, commit stages only SpecGuard-generated files) <!-- claim: mcp-activity-and-limits -->
- [ ] The GitHub Action installs the requested SpecGuard version, runs the chosen gates in a fixed order (status, drift, proof, align, results, validate, security, check, test, verify, scan; `deps` is an alias of `scan`), rejects an unknown gate before running anything, writes a job summary and per-gate JSON, and uploads `.specguard/` as evidence excluding secrets and auth state <!-- claim: action-gates -->
- [ ] `fail-on` thresholds (missing-specs, drift, proof-failed, proof-stale, proof-unexercised, proof-unproven, align-below:<n>, results, validate, security, check, test, verify, scan, deps, none) fail the job from the gates' exit codes; a gate that did not run, or a missing proof ledger, never fails the job <!-- claim: action-fail-on -->
- [ ] `mode: remediate` runs `specguard remediate` instead of the gates, adds `--pr` when asked, exposes the exit code, fails only on exit 1 or 11, and never merges; a release tag must equal the package version with the CLI published before the extension <!-- claim: action-remediate-and-release -->
- [ ] The VS Code extension adds an activity-bar sidebar and a singleton dashboard panel that run the CLI (resolved from a setting, a local binary or npx) and read `.specguard` files for coverage, pipeline status, drift, traceability and agent activity; commands needing a workspace report when none is open, the project can be switched, and no secrets are passed through <!-- claim: vscode-dashboard -->
- [ ] Optional behaviour is added through plugins named in `config.plugins`: a plugin may supply commands, catalog providers, implementation discoverers, external-id adapters, result sources, feature-state tuning, module stems and contract importers; an unknown or malformed plugin name is a configuration error where a pipeline loads it, and core never imports a plugin by name <!-- claim: plugin-contract -->
- [ ] The feature catalog (the `feature-catalog` plugin) is a directory of YAML parsed with a real YAML parser and validated against a schema (an unversioned or malformed file or a duplicate feature id is an error naming the file; `catalogFormat: list` reads bare lists); built-in GraphQL, REST and tRPC discoverers and the generic, Zephyr and Jira external-id adapters need no other plugin, and `specguard features` lists each spec's feature back-references <!-- claim: feature-catalog -->
- [ ] `features --state` reports per feature a summary, required channels and a state for UI, API and MCP (no, stub, built, broken, passing, proven) from specs, discovered implementations and test results matched by feature id, tag or external id, plus an agent gate that opens only on a latest passing unit or integration test; with no catalog it prints `[]` with a note and does not fail <!-- claim: feature-state -->
- [ ] `quality` runs ESLint and Knip (and Ruff for Python) for every app or one app, can auto-fix lint issues, normalises findings into `.specguard/code-quality.json` with error and warning totals, exits 2 only when lint errors exist, treats an unavailable tool as a warning, and rejects an unknown app name with the list of known ones <!-- claim: code-quality -->
- [ ] `commit` stages and commits only SpecGuard-generated paths (tests, docs, specs, `.specguard/` and the directories the config writes to), supports `--dry-run`, a custom message and an originating pipeline, reports a clean tree or nothing to commit with success, fails with exit 1 when git is missing or git add or commit fails, and appends each commit to `.specguard/changelog.md` <!-- claim: git-helpers -->
- [ ] The surface is small: `analyze`, `plan-fix` and `deps` are gone (`check`, `security scan` and the remediation plan replace them, and the Action's `deps` gate is an alias of `scan`), and the MCP server registers about 16 core tools (`check`, `spec_graph`, `read_spec`, `write_spec`, `history_add`, `history_log`, `test_run`, `verify`, `security_scan`, `security_plan`, `proof_status`, `results_ingest`, `impact`, `contracts`, `workspace_status`, `init`) while the pre-0.2 tool names register only when `SPECGUARD_MCP_LEGACY=1`; plugin tools always register <!-- claim: planned-reduced-surface -->
- [ ] Plugin commands are registered on the CLI as `specguard <name>` and on the MCP server as `specguard_<name>` (with typed inputs when the command declares them), only while the plugin is enabled; config is read before commands are parsed, core commands and tools win a name clash, and a plugin that cannot be loaded is reported once and skipped so `init` still works with a broken config <!-- claim: plugin-commands -->
- [ ] Plugins can add `detectors` (their findings become `code` items in the remediation plan under the owning capability, reported but never auto-patched, and closed only when the detector ran without warnings) and `docRenderers` (the docs API tries them before the model; a renderer that declines or fails falls through), and npm plugins load only from an explicit `{name, package}` allowlist in config, resolved from the project's own `node_modules`, because importing a package runs its code <!-- claim: planned-plugin-extensions -->
- [ ] `init --history-hooks` installs history hooks (into `.claude/settings.local.json`, personal and uncommitted) so prompts and plans are captured into the requirement history automatically, using the same safe, idempotent merge rules as the existing hooks <!-- claim: planned-history-hooks -->
- [ ] The feature catalog's layout is entirely `featureState` config (catalog directory and format, results directories, id rules, placeholder and MCP patterns, repo channels, module stems, and where agent tools are declared and which of them do not count); no platform's layout is built in, and a test fails if a customer platform is named anywhere in code, docs or specs <!-- claim: catalog-layout-config -->
- [ ] The `contract-mappings` plugin adds contract edges from a JSON file of spec-to-provider mappings whose location and key names are `contractMappings` config, with plain defaults, and yields nothing for a missing or malformed file <!-- claim: contract-mappings-importer -->
- [ ] Core reaches optional functionality only through enabled plugins: `quality` exists only when a plugin provides it, and core commands never run code quality themselves <!-- claim: core-plugin-boundary -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Bootstrap a project for humans and agents
**Steps:**
1. In a clean repository the developer runs `specguard init`.
2. They run it a second time.

**Expected Results:**
- The config, specs directory, `.env` placeholder, git-ignore block, agent instruction files and MCP and hook wiring exist, and stdout lists what was created and next steps.
- The second run reports every path as skipped and modifies nothing.
- No real secret is written.

### Scenario 2: Existing hook differs from the generated one
**Steps:**
1. The user has customised the post-edit hook in `.claude/settings.json`.
2. They run `specguard scaffold`.

**Expected Results:**
- A diff of old versus new is printed and the file is unchanged.
- Running `specguard scaffold --update-hooks` applies the change.
- Unrelated settings keys are preserved either way.

### Scenario 3: An agent drives SpecGuard over MCP
**Steps:**
1. An agent starts the MCP server and calls `specguard_status` then `specguard_drift`.
2. A call fails because of a bad argument.

**Expected Results:**
- Each call returns a text summary with counts and messages, and writes running and pass or fail entries to the activity log that the dashboard displays.
- The failed call returns an error result and the server keeps running.

### Scenario 4: Pull request gate in CI
**Steps:**
1. A workflow uses the Action with `gates: status,drift,proof` and `fail-on: drift,proof-failed`.
2. A pull request introduces drift.

**Expected Results:**
- The drift gate exits 3, the threshold trips and the job fails with a summary naming the tripped rule.
- Per-gate JSON and the evidence artifact are uploaded without secrets.
- A gate that was not requested cannot fail the job.

### Scenario 5: Misspelt plugin
**Steps:**
1. The config lists `plugins: ["typo"]`.
2. The user runs any command that loads plugins.

**Expected Results:**
- The CLI reports `plugins not loaded: unknown plugin 'typo'` once and registers none of that plugin's commands, and a pipeline that needs the plugin fails with a configuration error naming it.

### Scenario 6: Feature alignment report
**Steps:**
1. A catalog directory lists two features; tests and specs link to them.
2. The user runs `specguard features --state`.

**Expected Results:**
- Each feature shows its summary, required channels and a state per channel.
- A feature with only a passing end-to-end result has a proven channel, while one with a failing latest result shows broken.
- The agent gate is open only for a feature with a passing unit or integration test.

### Scenario 7: Commit generated files only
**Steps:**
1. The working tree contains new generated tests and an unrelated source change.
2. The user runs `specguard commit --dry-run`, then `specguard commit`.

**Expected Results:**
- The dry run lists what would be staged and changes nothing.
- The real run commits only the generated tests, skipping the source change, and logs the entry in `.specguard/changelog.md`.

## Security & Data Considerations
- Setup writes agent configuration files that can run commands (hooks and MCP servers), so it never overwrites an existing entry silently, prints a diff instead, and always writes the exact runner it resolved.
- `.specguard/.env` holds API keys; it contains only a placeholder at creation, is git-ignored by the managed block, and is excluded from CI evidence uploads along with auth state.
- Environment loading never overrides variables already set; logs and results never include key values.
- MCP tools run with the user's privileges but are limited to read, generate and report operations; remediation over MCP is read-only and the commit tool stages only generated files.
- Plugins are code. Built-in plugins load only by name from a known location, and the npm plugin loader accepts only an explicit `{name, package}` allowlist, with package names restricted to npm names (no paths or URLs), because importing a package executes it.
- The Action's token is only needed in remediate mode and only for push and pull request creation; nothing is ever merged.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard <command>` with global `--config`, `--json`, `--record`; setup commands `init` (`--with-playwright`, `--language`, `--harness claude|cursor|both`, `--single`, `--runner node|npx|path`, `--runner-path`, `--update-hooks`) and `scaffold`; plus the commands of enabled plugins: `features [--state] [--cases <file>]` (feature-catalog), `quality [--app] [--fix]` (quality), `commit [--dry-run] [--message] [--app] [--pipeline]` (git).
- MCP: binary `specguard-mcp` over stdio, tools named `specguard_<command>` (including `specguard_scaffold`, `specguard_read_spec`, `specguard_write_spec`), plus `specguard_<command>` for each enabled plugin command (`specguard_features`, `specguard_quality`, `specguard_commit`).
- Files written: `.specguard/config.json`, `.specguard/.env`, `.specguard/activity-log.json`, `.specguard/code-quality.json`, `.specguard/changelog.md`, `.specguard/ci/<gate>.json`, `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/skills/specguard/SKILL.md`, `.claude/commands/goal.md`, `.cursor/mcp.json`, `.cursor/skills/specguard/SKILL.md`.
- Config keys: `plugins`, `featureState` (catalog, catalogFormat, reporters, resultsDirs, externalIds, channelByType, repoChannels, moduleStems, idSkipSegments, placeholderSummaryPattern, mcpModulePattern, agentTools), `contractMappings`, `runners`, `llm.*`.
- GitHub Action inputs: `mode`, `gates`, `fail-on`, `results`, `run-id`, `drift-since`, `validate-url`, `version`, `working-directory`, `remediate-args`, `open-pr`, `github-token`, `upload-evidence`; output `remediate-exit`.

# Platform Foundation

## Problem & Value
A tool that reads whole repositories, calls paid language models and gates CI builds has to behave the same way in every command. If each pipeline loaded configuration its own way, handled model failures differently, scanned dependency folders, or invented its own exit codes, the tool would be unpredictable, expensive and unsafe to automate. It would also be impossible to test without a live model.

Platform Foundation is the shared engine underneath every other capability. It finds and validates configuration, gives every pipeline one model-access layer with retries, fallbacks, spend caps, usage accounting and deterministic replay, redacts sensitive text before it leaves the machine, reads and writes files safely, knows how to treat each language and framework, and reports outcomes through a small stable set of exit codes. Users get predictable cost and behaviour; maintainers get one place to fix cross-cutting problems.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs any SpecGuard command inside a repo and it finds the right `.specguard/config.json` without silently inheriting a parent repo's settings.
- A team lead sets a spend cap in config so a runaway pipeline stops instead of running up a bill, and CI sees a distinct exit code when that happens.
- A platform engineer routes the fast and frontier tiers to different models, and overrides one pipeline to use a stronger model.
- A test author records real model responses once with `--record` and replays them in CI with no network and no API key.
- A security reviewer relies on the redactor to mask emails, card numbers and tokens before page snapshots or prompts are sent to a model.
- A CI script branches on exit codes (2 validation failed, 3 drift, 5 security issues, 8 budget reached) to decide what to do next.
- A monorepo owner declares several apps in one config, each with its own language, spec directory and test runner.

## Requirements
- [ ] Configuration is found by searching upward from the working directory for `.specguard/config.json`, stopping at the repository boundary so a repo without its own config never inherits a parent repo's; no config yields a not-found error that names the search start and suggests `specguard init` <!-- claim: config-discovery -->
- [ ] Configuration is validated against one schema: invalid JSON or an invalid field fails with a readable invalid-config error, unknown keys and `_comment` are tolerated, and the directory that holds `.specguard/` is exposed to every pipeline as the root <!-- claim: config-validation -->
- [ ] A config may extend exactly one other config by explicit path (file or directory) and nothing else is inherited: keys merge one level deep, a child's `apps` and arrays replace the parent's, and a cycle or missing target is an invalid-config error <!-- claim: config-extends -->
- [ ] Config describes one or more apps, each with language, repo directory, spec directory, source globs, framework, test output, test command settings, entry points, exclusions and path-prefix stripping, plus top-level paths, granularity, plugin and validation settings; sensible defaults apply to anything omitted, including TypeScript as the default language <!-- claim: config-apps-and-defaults -->
- [ ] Glob expansion never descends into dependency, build or VCS directories (node_modules, dist, build, coverage, .next, .git) even when a pattern would reach them, returns only sorted, de-duplicated absolute file paths, and skips dot-files <!-- claim: default-glob-excludes -->
- [ ] Every model call goes through one layer that supports multiple providers, takes the API key only from a named environment variable, never logs or includes the key in an error, fails clearly on a missing key or unknown provider, and validates structured output against the caller's schema <!-- claim: llm-provider-layer -->
- [ ] Each model attempt has a timeout; retryable failures (timeouts, rate limits, server errors, network resets) are retried with exponential backoff and jitter a configurable number of times, while authentication, validation and missing-key failures are never retried <!-- claim: llm-timeout-retry -->
- [ ] After a target exhausts its attempts, an ordered fallback chain (global or per pipeline) is tried; a budget or disabled-model error never triggers fallback <!-- claim: llm-fallback-chain -->
- [ ] Named model tiers `fast` and `frontier` can be configured; pipelines that summarise, document or propose history use `fast` and those that cluster or review specs use `frontier`, a pipeline's own override wins over its tier, and the tier wins over the global default <!-- claim: llm-model-tiers -->
- [ ] A per-pipeline override can set provider, model, key variable, tier and fallback for one named pipeline, where the pipeline name comes from the running CLI command or MCP tool <!-- claim: llm-pipeline-overrides -->
- [ ] A hard spend cap on tokens, calls or estimated dollars applies per process run, or per request scope in a server (each scope has its own count, budget, config and user, so concurrent requests cannot spend or reset one another's): once reached or projected to be crossed, every later call in that run or scope fails with a budget error and the CLI exits 8 and says why; a scope's user and labels are sent to the provider, and its usage is reported to its callback <!-- claim: llm-budget-cap -->
- [ ] Every real call adds tokens, call count and estimated cost to a usage log, in total and per pipeline and model, using a built-in price table that config can override <!-- claim: llm-usage-log -->
- [ ] A replay provider serves recorded responses keyed by a hash of the prompt, system text and image bytes with no network call; a miss names the hash and how to record, and `--record` or config writes every real response so a later run reproduces it <!-- claim: llm-replay-record -->
- [ ] Setting the provider to `none` makes every model call fail with a disabled error without touching the network so deterministic-only runs work, and disallowing images rejects any call that carries them <!-- claim: llm-disabled-and-images -->
- [ ] The redactor masks emails, phone numbers, US social security numbers, Luhn-valid card numbers, bearer and basic credentials (a token-shaped value, never the words in prose such as "basic requirements"), JWTs, private-key blocks, `password=`-style assignments and common API-key shapes with fixed placeholders, in time linear in the input; projects can add patterns, blank page selectors and a hook, redaction applies to every text kind, and re-redacting already redacted text changes nothing <!-- claim: secret-redaction -->
- [ ] File access goes through small reader and writer helpers: reads return UTF-8 text and reject on a missing file, existence checks return false instead of throwing, and writes create intermediate directories and replace the file atomically (a temp file renamed over it, so a reader never sees half a write); sentinel-delimited regions let SpecGuard own part of a hand-written file without touching the rest, and generated run state is kept out of version control through a managed ignore block <!-- claim: filesystem-access -->
- [ ] Language and framework profiles describe source globs, test file naming, test command and result parsing for TypeScript, Python, Go, Rust and Java, detect the language from marker files with a fixed tie-break, and honour per-app prefix stripping when deriving feature names <!-- claim: language-profiles -->
- [ ] Failures use typed errors that carry an exit code (default 1), and exit codes are stable across releases: 0 success, 1 internal, 2 validation failed, 3 drift, 4 missing specs, 5 security issues, 7 heal failed, 8 budget exceeded, with remediation-specific codes 8 to 11 scoped to that command <!-- claim: errors-and-exit-codes -->
- [ ] One build version is reported everywhere: `--version` prints it, `--version --json` prints name, version and Node version on one line, and the MCP server and extension report the same value <!-- claim: single-version-source -->
- [ ] A glob names a path literally where it can: a parenthesised segment such as the Next.js route group `app/(authenticated)/page.tsx` matches the folder `(authenticated)` instead of being read as a glob group, while extglob forms (`!(a|b)`, `@(a|b)`) and already-escaped characters keep their meaning <!-- claim: glob-literal-parens -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Run inside a sub-repo with no config
**Steps:**
1. A developer has a parent folder with `.specguard/config.json` and a nested git repo with none.
2. The developer runs `specguard status` inside the nested repo.

**Expected Results:**
- The command fails with a not-found error naming the directory it searched from and suggesting `specguard init`.
- The parent config is not used.
- The exit code is 1.

### Scenario 2: Inherit a shared config on purpose
**Steps:**
1. A repo's config sets `"extends": "../shared"` and overrides `llm.budget` and `apps`.
2. A command loads the config.

**Expected Results:**
- Parent keys merge one level deep; the child's `apps` replace the parent's.
- If the shared config points back to the child, loading fails with an invalid-config error about the cycle.

### Scenario 3: A runaway pipeline hits the spend cap
**Steps:**
1. Config sets `llm.budget.maxCalls` to 20.
2. A developer runs `specguard reverse --all` on a large app.

**Expected Results:**
- After 20 calls, further calls fail with a budget error and the command stops.
- The CLI says the budget was reached and exits 8.
- The usage log shows the tokens, calls and estimated cost spent, by pipeline and model.

### Scenario 4: Deterministic CI with replay
**Steps:**
1. A developer runs a pipeline once with `--record`.
2. CI runs the same pipeline with `provider: "replay"` and no API key.
3. A later change alters a prompt.

**Expected Results:**
- CI reproduces the recorded output with no network call.
- After the prompt change, the miss error names the prompt hash and says how to record again.

### Scenario 5: Provider failure falls back
**Steps:**
1. Config sets a primary model and a two-entry fallback chain.
2. The primary returns server errors; the first fallback is healthy.

**Expected Results:**
- The primary is retried with backoff up to the configured limit.
- The first fallback then serves the request.
- An authentication error on the primary is not retried.

### Scenario 6: Sensitive text is masked before sending
**Steps:**
1. A validation run collects page text containing an email, a card number and a bearer token.
2. The text is redacted before being sent to a model.

**Expected Results:**
- Placeholders replace all three values.
- A project pattern for internal ticket ids also masks those.
- Running the redactor again on the result changes nothing.

### Scenario 7: Dependencies are never scanned
**Steps:**
1. An app's source glob is `**/*.ts` and the repo contains `node_modules` and `dist`.
2. Any pipeline expands the glob.

**Expected Results:**
- No path under `node_modules`, `dist`, `.git` or similar is returned.
- Results are sorted, unique and absolute.

## Security & Data Considerations
Config stores only the names of environment variables that hold keys and credentials, never their values; error messages and logs must not contain a resolved key. Prompts and page text can contain personal or secret data, so the redactor is the single gate before text leaves the machine, and the LLM layer supports a hard off switch (`provider: none`) and an image block for sensitive environments. Spend caps are a safety control as well as a cost control. Replay recordings contain prompts and responses and should be treated as repository content. Globs never reach dependency or VCS directories, which also keeps third-party code out of model prompts. Config loading never walks past the repo boundary, so a stray parent config cannot silently change behaviour. Config-selected plugin or hook modules execute code and are loaded only from paths the project names.

## Interfaces
- Files: `.specguard/config.json` (with optional `extends`), `.specguard/llm-usage.json`, `.specguard/replay/` (default replay directory), managed ignore block in `.gitignore`, sentinel regions in hand-written docs.
- Config keys: `apps[]`, `paths.*`, `granularity.*`, `plugins`, `llm.provider|model|apiKeyEnv`, `llm.models.fast|frontier`, `llm.pipelines.<name>`, `llm.fallback`, `llm.timeoutMs|retries|backoffMs`, `llm.budget.maxUsd|maxTokens|maxCalls`, `llm.pricing`, `llm.replay.*`, `llm.allowImages`, `validate.redaction.*`.
- CLI flags and output: `--config <path>`, `--record`, `--version`, `--version --json`, `--json`.
- Exit codes: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 as listed above; `remediate` uses 8 to 11 for its own outcomes.
- Providers: `anthropic`, `openai`, `replay`, `none`, plus any provider the layer registers.

## Out of Scope
- Deciding which specs exist or whether code satisfies them (other capabilities).
- Running tests or browsers; this capability only describes how to find the right command.
- Hosting a model gateway or managing API keys; it reads keys from the environment.
- Any customer or platform specific configuration; those live in project config or plugins.
