# Requirement History

## Problem & Value
Specs say what a system must do, but not why it says that. The reasoning lives in chat transcripts, pull request threads and people's memories, and it is gone by the time someone asks why a requirement exists or whether it may be removed. Git history records what changed in code, not the intent that drove the change, and AI-assisted development makes this worse because the most important decisions are made in prompts and plans that are never committed.

Requirement History keeps a committed, readable record of the prompts, approved plans and explicit decisions that shaped each capability, and links each entry to the capabilities it affects. Reviewers and auditors get the intent behind a change; new contributors and coding agents get context before they edit; and `check` can point at capabilities whose code changed with no recorded reason.

The folder `specs/history/` holds the entries, the `history:` frontmatter list back-links them from capabilities, and the commands, hooks and reporting below are built.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer finishes a design discussion and runs `specguard history add --decision "Use per-request budgets in the docs server" --affects documentation-api` so the reasoning is committed with the code.
- A developer opts a repo in with `specguard init --history-hooks`, and from then on every approved plan from a Claude Code session is saved as a history entry along with the prompts that led to it.
- A reviewer runs `specguard history log --capability security-and-remediation` to read the timeline of why that capability is the way it is.
- A tech lead runs `specguard check` and sees a list of capabilities whose sources changed with neither a history entry nor a spec edit.
- A coding agent reads the history entries linked from a capability spec before changing it, so it does not undo a deliberate decision.
- A security reviewer reads a history entry to confirm a requirement was a deliberate decision and not an accident.

## Requirements
- [ ] A history entry is a markdown file at `specs/history/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` whose frontmatter has id (equal to the file name without extension), date, kind (prompt, plan, decision or a combination such as prompt+plan), author, source and an `affects` list of capability ids or `system`, followed by the verbatim text of the prompt, plan or decision <!-- claim: history-entry-format -->
- [ ] History entries are not specs: the spec loader skips the history folder, entries never appear as nodes in the spec graph, and two entries created on the same day with the same slug get distinct ids <!-- claim: history-not-specs -->
- [ ] `history add` records a prompt (`--prompt`), an approved plan (`--plan <file>`) or a decision (`--decision`) as a new entry, taking the author from git config and the source from the caller (default `manual`), and refuses to add an entry with no content <!-- claim: history-add -->
- [ ] when `--affects <ids>` is given, `history add` validates each id against the spec graph and fails with exit 2 on an unknown capability id, writing nothing <!-- claim: history-add-affects -->
- [ ] when `--affects` is omitted, `history add` asks the fast model tier to propose affected capabilities from the entry text (and the working-tree diff when present), keeps only ids that exist in the spec graph, and falls back to `system` when the model is disabled or proposes nothing <!-- claim: history-affects-proposal -->
- [ ] `history add` appends the entry id to the `history:` list in the frontmatter of each affected capability spec, leaving the rest of the spec byte-for-byte unchanged and adding the id only once <!-- claim: history-backrefs -->
- [ ] Editing only the `history:` or `sources:` frontmatter of a spec never marks an existing proof stale, because proofs hash the claim text and normative sections and not back-references <!-- claim: history-backrefs-not-stale -->
- [ ] `history log` prints entries newest first with date, kind, title and affected capabilities; `--capability <id>` restricts it to entries affecting that capability, and `--json` prints the same data as JSON <!-- claim: history-log -->
- [ ] `specguard init --history-hooks` is the only way hooks are installed; without the flag no history hook is written, and a repeated run changes nothing, preserves hooks the user already has, and replaces a differing SpecGuard hook only with `--update-hooks` <!-- claim: history-hooks-opt-in -->
- [ ] a UserPromptSubmit hook runs `history inbox`, which reads the hook's JSON from stdin with a real JSON parser (so quotes and newlines survive), appends the redacted prompt keyed by `session_id` and `cwd` to an uncommitted inbox file, caps the inbox size, and never fails the user's prompt <!-- claim: history-inbox-capture -->
- [ ] every history hook prints nothing to stdout (stdout is injected into the model's context), uses the resolved local SpecGuard binary rather than a cold package download, and ends in a way that swallows its own failures <!-- claim: history-hooks-silent -->
- [ ] a PostToolUse hook on ExitPlanMode runs `history capture`, which takes the approved plan from the tool input (falling back to the session transcript), pairs it with only the inbox prompts from the same `session_id`, and writes one committed prompt+plan entry; prompts from sessions that never reach an approved plan are never committed <!-- claim: history-plan-capture -->
- [ ] prompt text is passed through the shared secret redactor both when it is written to the inbox and again when an entry is committed, so keys, tokens and personal data never reach `specs/history/` <!-- claim: history-redaction -->
- [ ] `check` reports each capability whose owned sources changed since its last history entry or spec edit without either, as an advisory finding that does not by itself fail the build unless the project opts in <!-- claim: history-check-gap -->
- [ ] The MCP server exposes `history_add` and `history_log` with the same behaviour as the CLI command so agents can record decisions directly <!-- claim: history-mcp-tool -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: The worked example in this repository
**Steps:**
1. A developer asks Claude Code to redesign SpecGuard around functional specs and four pillars, then approves the resulting plan on 2026-10-15.
2. The history hooks capture the session and write `specs/history/2026-10-15-functional-specs-and-four-pillars.md`.
3. The entry's `affects` list contains `system`, and later capability specs list the entry id in their `history:` frontmatter.

**Expected Results:**
- The entry has frontmatter `id`, `date: 2026-10-15`, `kind: prompt+plan`, `author`, `source: claude-code` and `affects`.
- The body contains the original prompt verbatim, any follow-up decisions and the approved plan.
- `history log --capability spec-authoring` lists the entry once the capability links to it.

### Scenario 2: Record a decision by hand
**Steps:**
1. A developer runs `specguard history add --decision "Docs responses are not streamed" --affects documentation-api`.
2. The developer runs `specguard history log --capability documentation-api`.

**Expected Results:**
- A new dated entry exists under `specs/history/` with kind `decision`.
- The documentation-api spec's `history:` list gains the entry id and nothing else in the file changes.
- No proof for that capability becomes stale.
- The log shows the new entry first.

### Scenario 3: Affected capabilities are proposed
**Steps:**
1. A developer runs `specguard history add --prompt "Add per-request LLM budgets"` without `--affects`.
2. The fast model proposes `documentation-api`, `platform-foundation` and a made-up id.

**Expected Results:**
- The two real ids are used; the made-up id is discarded.
- Both capabilities gain the back-reference.
- With the LLM disabled the entry is recorded against `system`.

### Scenario 4: Hook capture across concurrent sessions
**Steps:**
1. A repo has history hooks installed; two Claude Code sessions A and B are open.
2. Each session submits prompts; session A approves a plan, session B does not.

**Expected Results:**
- Both sessions' prompts land in the uncommitted inbox, redacted, tagged with their `session_id`.
- Exactly one entry is committed, containing session A's plan and only session A's prompts.
- Session B's prompts are not committed.
- The hooks printed nothing to stdout in either session.

### Scenario 5: A secret in a prompt
**Steps:**
1. A developer pastes an API key into a prompt, then approves the plan.

**Expected Results:**
- The inbox line and the committed entry both show a placeholder instead of the key.
- The key appears nowhere under `specs/history/`.

### Scenario 6: A change with no recorded reason
**Steps:**
1. A developer edits files owned by a capability and commits without touching its spec or adding a history entry.
2. The developer runs `specguard check`.

**Expected Results:**
- The capability is listed as changed without a history entry or spec edit.
- Adding a history entry or editing the spec clears the finding.

## Security & Data Considerations
Prompts routinely contain secrets, customer data and internal URLs. Redaction (the shared redactor) is applied twice: at inbox write and at commit time. The inbox lives under `.specguard/history/` and is gitignored; only a captured, redacted entry is ever committed. Hooks read untrusted JSON from stdin and must parse it, never interpolate it into a shell command. Entries are append-only records, so a leaked value that slips past redaction must be removed by editing the committed file and rotating the secret. Hooks are opt-in so a repo never records prompts without a deliberate choice.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard history add [--prompt <text>|--plan <file>|--decision <text>] [--affects <ids>]`, `specguard history log [--capability <id>] [--json]`, `specguard history inbox` and `specguard history capture` (read hook JSON on stdin, print nothing), `specguard init --history-hooks`, `specguard check` (history-gap finding).
- Files: `specs/history/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md` (committed), `.specguard/history/inbox.jsonl` (uncommitted), `history:` list in capability frontmatter.
- Hooks (opt-in with `init --history-hooks`): `UserPromptSubmit` and `PostToolUse` with matcher `ExitPlanMode`, written to `.claude/settings.local.json`.
- MCP: `history_add`, `history_log`.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 internal error, 2 validation failure (unknown capability id). Hook commands always exit 0.

## Out of Scope
- Capturing full chat transcripts or tool output; only prompts, approved plans and explicit decisions are kept.
- Replacing git history, issue trackers or pull request discussions.
- Supporting coding tools other than Claude Code hooks in the first version.
- Rewriting or deleting past entries automatically.

# Security Scanning and Remediation

## Problem & Value
Security review usually looks only at code. Many serious flaws are really missing or wrong requirements: an endpoint that never said who may call it, a data field nobody classified, a rate limit nobody specified. At the same time, vulnerable dependencies pile up because upgrading them is risky: nobody knows whether the upgrade changes behaviour, so the work is postponed. Findings arrive in a dozen tool-specific formats and fix plans are ad hoc, so no other system (a ticket tracker, a remediation bot, a dashboard) can reliably consume them.

This capability finds security problems in code, dependencies, secrets and the specs themselves. It turns the findings into fixes that are proven safe: a vulnerable dependency or code finding is patched in a throwaway copy of the repo, the project's own tests and the proof ledger are compared before and after, and the change is proposed with a PRESERVED, CHANGED or INCONCLUSIVE behaviour verdict. A person always merges. It also publishes one stable remediation plan format so that other systems can read plans and report progress back.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard security --all --with-sast` to get OWASP-annotated security test stubs for each spec, plus Semgrep findings and a dependency audit, and sees exit code 5 when real findings exist.
- A CI pipeline runs `specguard remediate --scan-only` on a schedule and fails when advisories at or above a severity threshold remain.
- A maintainer runs `specguard remediate --pr` and receives one branch and pull request per advisory group, each with a behaviour verdict and an evidence report, and merges the PRESERVED ones.
- A reviewer reads the evidence report for a CHANGED verdict to see exactly which previously passing test or proven claim regressed.
- A security engineer runs `security scan` and gets code, dependency, secret and spec-level findings in one plan that an external tracker ingests, and marks items fixed through `security plan set-status`.

## Requirements
- [ ] `security` generates OWASP-annotated vitest security test stubs from a spec's security notes and its source module, for one spec (`--spec`) or all specs (`--all`); each generated test carries an `// OWASP A0X: <category>` comment, accidental Markdown fences are removed, an existing security test file is never overwritten (the spec is reported as skipped), and an LLM failure for one spec is recorded as failed without stopping the others <!-- claim: owasp-test-stubs -->
- [ ] `security --with-sast` runs Semgrep in a Docker container over each app's repo and the language-appropriate dependency audit (npm or pip); when Docker, Semgrep or the audit tool is unavailable it logs a warning and continues with zero findings instead of failing <!-- claim: sast-degrades-gracefully -->
- [ ] Real SAST or audit findings are summarised into the LLM prompt so generated stubs target concrete issues; `security` exits 5 only when real findings exist (generating stubs alone exits 0) and writes a structured report to `.specguard/security.json` with every finding, counts by severity and one row per spec handled, a report failure never changing the outcome <!-- claim: security-exit-and-report -->
- [ ] `remediate` detects dependency advisories through the ecosystem's native audit and OSV, Semgrep findings and gitleaks secrets; advisories are merged across tools by id or alias keeping the highest severity, suppressed by an ignore file with expiry dates, sorted deterministically and filtered by a minimum severity (default high) <!-- claim: unified-detection -->
- [ ] `remediate --scan-only` changes nothing and exits 5 when any advisory remains after suppression and thresholding, otherwise 0; secrets are only ever reported, never auto-fixed <!-- claim: scan-only-and-secrets -->
- [ ] A remediation run refuses a dirty working tree and a fresh lock, does all work in a temporary git worktree and never touches the user's working tree, and rolling back removes the worktree and branch <!-- claim: worktree-isolation -->
- [ ] The baseline runs the tests twice to quarantine flaky tests, snapshots the proof ledger, and a baseline that is not green ends the run with exit 11 before any patch is applied <!-- claim: green-baseline-required -->
- [ ] The planner chooses the smallest fixing version (patch over minor, major only with `--allow-major`), changes only manifests and lockfiles for a dependency bump or only the files named in a code finding, and aborts and rolls back on any other changed file <!-- claim: minimal-write-allowlist -->
- [ ] After patching, the install, build, typecheck and tests run (claim-tagged tests for the affected specs first, then the full suite), the detector runs again, and heal is never run in rewrite mode so no test file is modified <!-- claim: verify-after-patch -->
- [ ] The behaviour verdict compares proof-ledger results before and after: it is CHANGED when a baseline-passing test fails or vanishes, a proven claim drops, claim or test counts fall, an advisory remains or a new one appears, or build or typecheck is red; INCONCLUSIVE when output is unparseable, no tests were selected or proofs were not re-proven; otherwise PRESERVED, with CHANGED beating INCONCLUSIVE beating PRESERVED <!-- claim: behaviour-verdict -->
- [ ] Remediation runs use one branch per advisory group named `specguard/remediate/<id>`, skip advisories whose branch or PR already exists, and write the plan, diffs, selected tests, verdict and evidence to `.specguard/remediation/<runId>.json` with a markdown pull request body <!-- claim: branch-and-evidence -->
- [ ] Without `--pr` nothing is pushed; with `--pr` the branch is pushed and a pull request opened (normal for PRESERVED, draft for CHANGED or INCONCLUSIVE); `--dry-run` leaves no branch, push, PR or report in the user's tree; there is no auto-merge anywhere <!-- claim: pr-modes-no-merge -->
- [ ] `remediate` exits 8 for PRESERVED, 9 for CHANGED, 10 for INCONCLUSIVE and 11 for a setup or baseline error, and a missing external tool is reported by name as a warning rather than a raw error <!-- claim: remediate-exit-codes -->
- [ ] `security scan` runs the dependency-advisory, Semgrep and gitleaks detectors that `remediate` uses, as one detector set whose results share one finding shape; the older `security --with-sast` command remains for CI gates, and the retired `deps` gate is an alias of it <!-- claim: unified-scan -->
- [ ] `security scan` also performs a spec-level review per capability, flagging missing authorization or data-classification requirements, unspecified abuse cases or rate limits, contradictory requirements, interfaces with no owning claim, and code findings that reveal a spec gap; each finding has a type of spec, code, dependency or secret <!-- claim: spec-review -->
- [ ] Scans emit a `RemediationPlan` validated by one Zod schema and published as JSON Schema at `schemas/remediation-plan.v1.json`; each item carries finding references, severity, capability and claim links, the workspace unit when the project has a manifest, affected files, a change type (code, spec, dependency or config), the claims that must stay proven, an optional external reference, and a status that moves open, planned, in-progress, fixed, then verified or wont-fix <!-- claim: remediation-plan -->
- [ ] Plans are stored at `.specguard/security/plans/<id>.json`, served by the documentation API, and updated by other systems with `security plan set-status`; `security fix` executes plan items through the remediate executor and updates their status <!-- claim: plan-lifecycle -->
- [ ] A plan item's id is stable across scans (derived from what was found), so a later scan keeps its status, history and external reference; an item marked fixed or verified that the scanner reports again is reopened with a note; an unresolved item no longer detected is closed as fixed with the note "no longer detected" only when a detector that could have seen it ran at a severity floor covering it (a missing detector, a raised floor, an `--app` filter or a failed model review closes nothing, and spec findings are never closed by silence), a plan that cannot be read stops the scan instead of dropping every status, and items already closed and gone are dropped <!-- claim: plan-carry-over -->
- [ ] `security plan set-status` enforces the lifecycle: any state can be reopened, verified is reachable only from fixed, an unknown status, plan or item is rejected, and a stored plan that does not match the schema is never trusted; plans live behind one store interface (files by default) that serialises concurrent updates, and an update may carry the item version the caller last saw (the count of its recorded status changes), in which case a changed item is refused as a conflict and nothing is written <!-- claim: plan-transitions -->
- [ ] Resolving a spec-level item records a requirement-history decision against its capability, once <!-- claim: spec-fix-history -->
- [ ] A secret finding records only its rule and location, never the detector's message, so a plan can be handed to another system without carrying the secret <!-- claim: plan-no-secret-values -->
- [ ] `security fix` runs the remediation executor once for the selected dependency and code items, moves each item by what happened to its branch (preserved: fixed; changed: in-progress with the verdict; failed: open; skipped: planned; not attempted: open), records the branch in the item's history, re-reads the plan before writing so a status or external reference a tracker set meanwhile is kept, restores the items if the run crashes, and never patches spec or secret items <!-- claim: security-fix-statuses -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Safe dependency upgrade
**Steps:**
1. A project has a vulnerable direct dependency, a passing test suite and a clean working tree.
2. The developer runs `specguard remediate --pr`.

**Expected Results:**
- The patch is applied in a temporary worktree on branch `specguard/remediate/<id>` and only manifests and lockfiles change.
- Tests before and after match, so the verdict is PRESERVED.
- A normal (non-draft) pull request is opened with the evidence summary and the command exits 8.

### Scenario 2: Upgrade changes behaviour
**Steps:**
1. The patched dependency changes a function that a currently passing test relies on.
2. The developer runs `specguard remediate --pr`.

**Expected Results:**
- The baseline-passing test fails in the patched run and is listed by id.
- The verdict is CHANGED, a draft pull request lists the differences, and the command exits 9.
- The user's own working tree is untouched.

### Scenario 3: Scheduled gate on advisories
**Steps:**
1. CI runs `specguard remediate --scan-only --min-severity high` nightly.
2. One advisory is covered by an unexpired ignore entry and another is not.

**Expected Results:**
- The ignored advisory is reported as ignored with its reason and expiry.
- The other advisory is listed and the job exits 5.
- After the ignore entry expires, it stops suppressing.

### Scenario 4: Unreliable baseline
**Steps:**
1. The project's test suite fails on the unmodified code, or its output cannot be parsed.
2. The developer runs `specguard remediate`.

**Expected Results:**
- No patch is applied and the worktree is removed.
- The command exits 11 and explains that the baseline is not green.
- Tests whose status differed between the two baseline runs are reported as flaky and excluded.

### Scenario 5: Security stubs with SAST unavailable
**Steps:**
1. A developer runs `specguard security --all --with-sast` on a machine without Docker.

**Expected Results:**
- A warning says the SAST scan could not run, and no exception is thrown.
- Stubs are still written under `tests/security/`, existing ones are skipped, and the exit code is 0.

### Scenario 6: Spec-level finding becomes a tracked plan item
**Steps:**
1. `security scan` reviews a capability whose interface accepts uploads but has no authorization requirement.
2. The resulting plan is written to `.specguard/security/plans/<id>.json` and an external tracker imports it.
3. After the spec is amended, the tracker runs `security plan set-status` for the item.

**Expected Results:**
- The item has finding type spec, change type spec, a link to the capability, and status open.
- The tracker's update moves it to fixed and a later verification moves it to verified.
- The schema file `schemas/remediation-plan.v1.json` validates the plan.

## Security & Data Considerations
- The pipelines read source files, dependency manifests and test results, and send file contents or finding summaries to the configured LLM only for stub generation, spec-level review, changelog analysis and code fixes. Only the file named by a finding is sent for a code fix. LLM keys are referenced by environment variable name and never logged or written to reports.
- Secrets reported by gitleaks are redacted and are never auto-fixed or committed; they must be rotated by a person. Reports under `.specguard/` can contain package names and file paths and should be treated as internal.
- LLM-suggested edits are untrusted input: remediation limits writes with an allowlist and file and line limits, and `security fix` is the only thing that applies a plan item.
- Remediation never merges, never rewrites tests, and works only in a temporary worktree. The MCP remediate tool is limited to scan-only and dry-run because branch, push and pull-request creation have effects outside the machine.
- Semgrep and OSV run through Docker or local binaries; a missing tool degrades to a warning.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard security [--spec <key>] [--all] [--with-sast] [--app] [--force]`, `specguard remediate [--scan-only] [--advisory <id>] [--min-severity critical|high|moderate|low] [--allow-major] [--ledger <file>] [--pr|--no-pr] [--dry-run] [--no-llm] [--app] [--force]`.
- CLI: `security scan [--min-severity <level>] [--no-spec-review] [--app <name>]`, `security fix [plan] [--item <id>] [--pr] [--dry-run] [--no-llm] [--allow-major]`, `security plan list|show|set-status`.
- MCP tools: `specguard_security`, `specguard_security_scan`, `specguard_security_plan`, `specguard_remediate` (scan-only and dry-run only).
- Files: `tests/security/<feature>.test.ts`, `.specguard/security.json`, `.specguard/vuln-ignore.json` (id, reason, expires), `.specguard/remediate.lock`, `.specguard/remediation/<runId>.json` and `.specguard/remediation/<runId>/baseline-proofs.json`, `.specguard/rules/semgrep/` (optional custom rules). Planned: `.specguard/security/plans/<id>.json`, `schemas/remediation-plan.v1.json`.
- Config: `remediate` block (`minSeverity`, `maxAdvisories`, `maxFilesChanged`, `maxLinesChanged`, build, typecheck and install commands, `osv`, `semgrep`, `gitleaks`), per-app `security` settings.
- Exit codes: security and security scan use 5 for security issues; remediate uses 8 PRESERVED, 9 CHANGED, 10 INCONCLUSIVE, 11 setup or baseline error (8 is the budget-exceeded code for other commands).
- GitHub Action: `mode: remediate` and the `security` and `scan` gates (`deps` is kept as an alias of `scan`) (see the integration-surfaces capability).

## Out of Scope
- Auto-merging any change, or rewriting or deleting tests to make a patch pass.
- Auto-fixing or rotating leaked secrets.
- Replacing a dedicated vulnerability management or ticketing system; plans are consumed by those systems.
- A general-purpose SAST engine: Semgrep, OSV, gitleaks and ecosystem audit tools do the detection.
- Planned and deferred: an HTTP write endpoint for plan status (updates go through the CLI first).

# Spec Authoring

## Problem & Value
Code changes quickly, often written by AI agents, and the intent behind it does not survive. Without a written, structured description of what a system is for and what it must do, tests drift, documentation goes stale and reviewers have nothing to judge the code against. Teams with an existing codebase or a pile of requirement documents rarely have the time to write specs from scratch, and specs that mirror individual source files are too granular to say anything about value.

Spec Authoring gives every other SpecGuard capability something solid to stand on. It defines the spec format (a master system spec, functional capability specs, optional components and journeys), gives each requirement a stable claim id, records which code a spec owns, and validates the whole set as a tree. It also bootstraps specs from existing code or outside documents, so a brownfield system can adopt spec-driven development in hours instead of weeks.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard reverse --all` on an existing codebase to get first-draft specs, then edits them into capability specs.
- A product owner runs `specguard import prd.md` to turn a requirements document into specs that become the new source of truth.
- A tech lead runs `specguard spec graph` to see the system, capability and component tree, which files each spec owns, and which rules are broken.
- A developer runs `specguard claims assign` after adding requirements so every bullet gets a stable id that tests and proofs can cite.
- A QA lead runs `specguard claims list --workspace` in CI to fail the build when a journey cites a claim that no longer exists.
- A coding agent reads a capability spec, including its declared sources, before editing the code that spec owns.
- A maintainer runs `specguard index` to produce an architecture index of the routes or endpoints and the spec tree.

## Requirements
- [ ] A spec may declare its metadata in YAML frontmatter (id, kind, title, parent, value, status, sources, tests, docs, history); frontmatter is read first, and specs that use the older HTML-comment metadata block still parse unchanged <!-- claim: frontmatter-v2-metadata -->
- [ ] Invalid frontmatter (bad YAML, a kind other than system, capability, component or journey, a non-string where a string is required, a list of non-strings) fails with an error that names the file and explains that lists must be block lists with quoted globs <!-- claim: frontmatter-errors -->
- [ ] A spec parses into a title, named sections, scenarios (name, numbered steps, expected-result bullets) and claims; missing sections yield empty values rather than errors, unknown metadata keys are preserved, and `Requirements` is accepted as the preferred name for `Acceptance Criteria` <!-- claim: sections-and-scenarios -->
- [ ] Spec discovery walks the specs tree recursively for markdown files, ignoring `README.md` files, the requirement-history folder and archived v1 specs, and parsing itself never touches the network or the filesystem beyond reading files <!-- claim: spec-discovery -->
- [ ] Every spec has one canonical key: its path relative to the specs root without the extension (or the owning app's spec directory when there is no specs root), used identically by claims, proofs, drift, the matrix and status <!-- claim: canonical-spec-key -->
- [ ] A spec's declared `sources` globs are resolved relative to the owning app's repo; a pattern that matches nothing there but matches from the config root is accepted with a one-time warning per pattern <!-- claim: declared-sources -->
- [ ] A requirement bullet carries its stable id in a trailing claim comment; bullets without one remain visible as unanchored, and reordering bullets never changes what an id refers to <!-- claim: claim-anchors -->
- [ ] `claims assign` adds an id to every requirement bullet that lacks one, never rewrites an existing id, generates lowercase unique slugs of at most six words and 48 characters, is idempotent, and with `--dry-run` reports the ids without writing <!-- claim: claims-assign -->
- [ ] `claims list` prints the claim catalog (optionally across every repo in the workspace) and exits 2 when a journey cites a claim that does not exist or a spec repeats a claim id <!-- claim: claims-list-gate -->
- [ ] A journey spec declares its world, actors and goals, invariants and budget, and each invariant lists the claim references it verifies, written as `specKey#claimId` or `repo:specKey#claimId` <!-- claim: journey-specs -->
- [ ] The spec graph arranges every spec as a tree (system, capability, component), attaches a capability with no parent to the system, keeps v1 specs as untyped nodes, and `spec graph` prints each node with its kind, owned-file count and claim count <!-- claim: graph-tree -->
- [ ] The graph answers which specs own a given file (zero, one or several) and which files are unowned, based only on declared sources, and ignores dependency and build directories <!-- claim: graph-file-ownership -->
- [ ] `spec graph` reports as errors a missing or multiple system spec, a missing id, an id that differs from the file name, a duplicate id, an unknown parent, a parent cycle, a wrong parent kind, a duplicate claim id and a missing Problem & Value section, and exits 2 on any error; it reports as warnings a spec whose sources match no files and a capability count above the configured maximum <!-- claim: graph-validation -->
- [ ] `reverse` requires either `--app <name>` or `--all` (exit 1 with a message otherwise), generates specs from the app's discovered source files, skips existing specs unless `--force`, supports `--file` for one source file, and ends with a created/updated/skipped/failed summary <!-- claim: reverse-per-source -->
- [ ] `reverse` keeps going when one spec or app fails, exits with the last non-zero code, caps each file sent to the model at 20,000 characters, never walks dependency or build directories, and warns about source files that look like they contain secrets while instructing the model not to reproduce them <!-- claim: reverse-safety -->
- [ ] `import` converts a local markdown or text file, or an http(s) URL, into spec files: a multi-section document is decomposed into a set of focused specs unless `--single` or `--out` is given, existing specs are skipped unless `--force`, and the result summary and exit code reflect created, skipped and failed items <!-- claim: import-documents -->
- [ ] `index` writes an architecture index at the root of the specs tree listing routes or endpoints grouped by area plus a spec directory map, finds the routing source through the app's entry points or detected framework, leaves an existing index alone unless `--force`, and writes a skeleton index instead of failing when the model call fails <!-- claim: index-generation -->
- [ ] `spec draft` inventories the code, summarises each file with the fast model (cached by content hash), clusters it into about 8 to 15 functional capabilities (honouring `granularity.target` and any `--guidance` the maintainers give, retrying once when the count misses it without losing the guidance), writes a reviewable capability map to `.specguard/spec-map.json` and `.md` outside `plans/`, and stops there unless `--yes` is given; `--from-map` continues from the edited map and writes one spec per capability plus the system spec <!-- claim: spec-draft-proposes-map -->
- [ ] `spec index` regenerates only the marked Capability Map region of the system spec from the spec graph and leaves the rest of the file untouched; `import <file> --capability <id>` adds only the requirements a document states that the capability does not already cover (a dry run unless `--yes`), appends them with unique claim anchors, and records a history entry for what it changed <!-- claim: spec-index-refreshes-map -->
- [ ] `spec consolidate` clusters existing per-file specs into capability specs, assigns every old spec to exactly one capability (otherwise it stops and lists the unassigned ones), merges their requirements with unique claim ids that never use numeric suffixes, carries over every old claim with an id that the model did not absorb (a bullet that never had an id has no reference to preserve and is superseded by the model's functional requirements), then rewrites claim tags in tests, rekeys the proof ledger and drift registry, archives the old specs under `_archive/v1`, and writes `.specguard/claim-migration.json` so results carrying old tags are still accepted on ingest <!-- claim: spec-consolidate-migrates-state -->
- [ ] `spec tag` links existing tests to requirements: for each capability the model is shown its requirements and the leaf tests in the files its `tests:` globs name, and says which requirements each test clearly exercises; only real requirement ids and test numbers survive, a `[claims: ...]` comment is written above the test in the file's comment style (a test already tagged is never touched, and two capabilities citing one test are merged into one comment), the run is a dry run unless `--yes`, and it reports which requirements no test covers <!-- claim: spec-tag-links-tests -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Adopt specs on an existing codebase
**Steps:**
1. A developer runs `specguard reverse --all` in a repo that has no specs.
2. The developer re-runs the same command without `--force`.
3. The developer runs `specguard claims assign` and then `specguard spec graph`.

**Expected Results:**
- First run creates specs and prints a summary such as `reverse: N created, 0 updated, 0 skipped, 0 failed`.
- Second run skips every existing spec and calls no model.
- Every requirement bullet now has a claim id and the graph lists each spec with its claim count.
- No spec is generated for anything inside `node_modules`, `dist` or `.git`.

### Scenario 2: Import a requirements document
**Steps:**
1. A product owner runs `specguard import docs/prd.md --app web`, where the PRD has several top-level sections.
2. The owner runs the command again without `--force`.

**Expected Results:**
- The document is decomposed into several focused specs in the app's spec directory, with file names derived from their titles.
- The second run reports them as skipped and overwrites nothing.
- The process exit code equals the pipeline's exit code (0 on success).

### Scenario 3: Validate the spec tree
**Steps:**
1. A developer adds a capability spec whose `id` differs from its file name and whose `parent` names a spec that does not exist.
2. The developer runs `specguard spec graph`.
3. The developer fixes the spec and runs the command again.

**Expected Results:**
- The first run prints `[error]` lines for `id-filename` and `unknown-parent` and exits with code 2.
- The second run prints the tree with no errors and exits 0; a spec whose sources match nothing still shows only a `[warn]`.

### Scenario 4: Catch a dangling journey claim
**Steps:**
1. A journey spec has an invariant that verifies `payments/checkout#charge-once`.
2. A developer renames that claim id in the capability spec.
3. CI runs `specguard claims list --workspace`.

**Expected Results:**
- The command reports the missing reference against the invariant.
- It exits with code 2, failing the build.

### Scenario 5: Find who owns a file
**Steps:**
1. Two capability specs declare overlapping source globs; a third file under `src/` matches no spec.
2. A tool asks the graph which specs own each file.

**Expected Results:**
- The shared file returns both spec ids; the unmatched file is reported as unowned.
- Files under dependency or build directories are never reported.

### Scenario 6: Bad frontmatter is explained
**Steps:**
1. A developer writes `sources: [src/{a,b}/**]` as a flow list in a capability spec.
2. A command that loads specs is run.

**Expected Results:**
- The error names the spec file and says lists must be block lists with quoted globs.
- Other specs that are valid are not silently dropped without a message.

## Security & Data Considerations
`reverse` and `import` send source code or document text to the configured LLM provider, so they run through the shared LLM layer (budget caps, redaction, replay) and instruct the model never to reproduce secret values. `reverse` warns before sending a file that matches secret patterns. `import` fetches only http and https URLs, follows at most one redirect, and refuses other schemes; it must not forward credentials found in a document to the model. Generated files are written only inside the repo's spec directories (or the explicit `--out` path). Parsing is pure and executes no code from specs.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard reverse [--app <name>|--all] [--file <path>] [--force] [--collapse <globs>]`, `specguard import <file|url> [--app] [--out] [--force]`, `specguard index [--app] [--force]`, `specguard claims assign [--dir] [--dry-run]`, `specguard claims list [--workspace]`, `specguard spec graph`.
- Spec files: `specs/**/*.md` with YAML frontmatter (v2) or an HTML-comment metadata block (v1); claim anchors written as an HTML comment holding `claim:` and a kebab-case id.
- Config keys: `paths.specsRoot`, `apps[].specDir`, `apps[].sources`, `apps[].exclude`, `apps[].collapse`, `granularity.target`, `granularity.maxCapabilities`.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 internal error or missing flags, 2 validation failure (graph errors, dangling or duplicate claims).
- `specguard spec draft [--yes] [--from-map] [--force] [--history <ids...>] [--guidance <text>]`, `specguard spec consolidate [--yes] [--from-map] [--force] [--no-archive] [--rewrite-source-refs] [--guidance <text>]`, `specguard spec index`, `specguard spec graph`, `specguard spec tag [--spec <id>] [--yes]`.

## Out of Scope
- Judging whether code satisfies a spec (see traceability and conformance capabilities).
- Recording the prompts and plans behind a spec (see requirement-history).
- Rendering specs as user or developer documentation.
- Writing specs that describe third-party dependencies.

# Local-first operation with an optional team server

## Problem & Value
A tool that checks code against its specs is most useful when everyone sees the same answer. A developer's laptop knows their working tree and nothing else. CI knows what was pushed, but its results vanish with the build. Auditors, product owners and reviewers have no checkout at all. Putting everything on a server would make SpecGuard useless on a plane, in a fresh clone, or the moment the server is down; keeping everything local leaves the team without a shared record of what is proven, what is stale, and which security findings are being worked.

This capability keeps one engine and gives it two homes. The local command line is always complete. A team server is optional: it holds what CI publishes, serves the same API the local `serve` does, shares generated documents and remediation plans, and attributes model spend to the person who asked. Every client (the command line, the MCP server, the VS Code extension, the web UI) talks to the same project-scoped API, and uses the server when it answers and local files when it does not. Git remains the source of truth for specs and requirement history; the server only indexes and aggregates them.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard check` and sees the team's CI proofs next to their own local ones, and keeps working unchanged when the server is unreachable.
- CI runs `specguard publish` after the tests, so the server shows the proof state of the commit that was pushed.
- A security lead reads the open findings from the server, and a tracker marks items in progress or fixed through the API without overwriting anyone else's change.
- An auditor or product owner with no checkout reads the system guide, capability docs and traceability from the server's web UI.

## Requirements
- [ ] `specguard publish` writes one snapshot file holding the spec and history markdown, the trace model, the proof rows, the newest remediation plan and the contract graph, tagged with the project name, repository, branch, commit, origin and engine and hash versions; it never includes source code, working-tree files outside the spec tree, or prompts that were not committed as history, and it redacts credentials from every file; with `--push` or `--server` it also sends the snapshot to the project's team server, and a refusal or an unreachable server fails the command while the file is still written <!-- claim: publish-snapshot -->
- [ ] A snapshot is validated before it is written or accepted: the project name is a safe identifier, every file is a markdown file inside the spec tree (no absolute paths, `..` or backslashes), the trace model has its required shape, an unknown version is refused, and anything over the size limit is refused <!-- claim: snapshot-validation -->
- [ ] The API serves every project under `/api/v1/projects/:project/...`, lists projects at `/api/v1/projects`, and on a server with one project also serves the same routes without the prefix; a server with several projects answers an unprefixed route with a pointer to the prefixed form; besides the existing routes it serves specs with their file (and one spec's markdown), coverage per capability and unit, the document list, the contract graph and unresolved findings, and the web UI works under a path prefix and across projects <!-- claim: project-scoped-api -->
- [ ] The API reports `apiVersion`, `engineVersion`, `hashVersion` and whether it accepts writes on `/health` and `/version`, so a client can refuse to mix incompatible data <!-- claim: version-handshake -->
- [ ] A registry that is not writable (the local `serve`) answers every write with 405; on a writable one a plan item is changed with `PATCH` by a signed-in maintainer, the change is attributed to them, a stale `If-Match` version is refused with 409 and writes nothing, and a lifecycle violation is refused with 422 <!-- claim: guarded-writes -->
- [ ] A team server keeps its state behind one backend interface (snapshots, plans per project, a document cache per project, tokens, an audit trail and model usage), implemented for files and for Postgres and held to the same contract tests; a project is shown from its newest snapshot on the default branch, else its newest overall; concurrent edits to plans lose nothing, with Postgres using a revision check and retry instead of row locks <!-- claim: team-server-storage -->
- [ ] Every route except `/health` needs a credential: a token (a person's, a project's CI token, or the operator's bootstrap token) or, for browsers, the sandbox's signed-in user header, which reads and mints a person's own tokens but never grants an administrative power; a bad token is refused even when the header is present; a project-scoped credential reaches only its project; nobody mints a token more powerful than their own, admin tokens come only from the admin route; tokens are stored as hashes, shown once, revocable by their owner, and audited; changes made from a browser session need the `X-Requested-With` header <!-- claim: team-server-auth -->
- [ ] A project's CI token or a maintainer publishes a snapshot over HTTP, creating the project on first publish; the snapshot's plan is merged with the stored one, so statuses and tracker references that people set on the server survive a republish, an item marked fixed that a scan sees again reopens, and unresolved items the new plan lacks are kept unless that plan was made from the stored one <!-- claim: team-server-publish -->
- [ ] Documents on a team server are generated once per spec content, audience, prompt version and model and shared by everyone, and each generation runs in its own model scope with the requester's name, the project and the gateway's labels, so spend is attributed to the person who asked and recorded per user and project <!-- claim: team-server-docs -->
- [ ] The server fetches the `specguard-evidence` artifacts CI uploaded for each configured repository on a timer, publishes the snapshot inside under the configured project with the commit and branch taken from the workflow run, skips what it already has and artifacts that are expired, oversized, invalid or from forks, and reports one repository's failure without stopping the others <!-- claim: artifact-puller -->
- [ ] The server answers MCP over HTTP at `/mcp` for token holders only, as read-only tools (projects, system, capability, spec, audit, coverage, docs, history, findings, plans) that go through the same API as the same identity, so access rules, project scoping and redaction are the API's <!-- claim: remote-mcp -->
- [ ] Commands that can use a server resolve it from config or the environment, check its health with a short timeout and a compatible API version, and otherwise behave locally: reads fall back silently and say which source they used; a shared write goes to the server or, with none, is written locally and marked local-only; a server that answers but refuses (bad token, no permission, lifecycle violation) is an error and never a quiet switch to local; `server.mode: required` makes an unreachable server an error and `off` never contacts it; `check --team`, the plan commands, the MCP plan tool and the VS Code extension all follow this, and a token saved by `login` is checked against the server before it is kept <!-- claim: local-first-fallback -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: CI publishes a commit
**Steps:**
1. CI runs the tests and ingests the results.
2. CI runs `specguard publish`.

**Expected Results:**
- One snapshot file exists with the spec files, trace, proofs and plan.
- The file contains no source code and no credential values.

### Scenario 2: Two people update a finding at once
**Steps:**
1. Two trackers read the same plan item at version 2.
2. Both send a status change with `If-Match: 2`.

**Expected Results:**
- The first succeeds and the item moves to version 3.
- The second receives 409 and the item keeps the first change.

## Security & Data Considerations
Only specs, history entries, trace data, proof rows and plans leave a machine, and only when `publish` runs. Source code and uncommitted prompts never do. Credentials are redacted from every file before the snapshot is written, and again from every response the API serves. Writes require a signed-in maintainer; the user recorded on a change is the authenticated one, never a name sent in the request body.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard publish [--out <file>] [--project <name>] [--push] [--server <url>] [--token <t>]`, `specguard server [--port] [--host] [--base-path] [--data-dir]`, `specguard login|logout [--server <url>] [--token <t>]`, `specguard check --team`.
- Server: `/mcp` (MCP over HTTP, token only), `POST /api/v1/projects/:project/snapshots`, `GET|POST|DELETE /api/v1/tokens`, `POST /api/v1/admin/tokens`.
- API: `GET /api/v1/projects`, `GET /api/v1/projects/:project/{system,capabilities,specs,specs/:id,coverage,trace,audit,units,contracts,findings,docs,security/plans}`, `PATCH /api/v1/projects/:project/security/plans/:plan/items/:item`.
- Config: `server: { url, project, tokenEnv, mode, timeoutMs }`.
- Files: `.specguard/publish/snapshot.json`.

## Out of Scope
- Running tests on the server: tests need the project's own environment, so CI runs them and publishes the result.
- Holding anyone's working tree: the server reads only published snapshots.
- Not built yet: live change notifications (clients poll or watch files), reading the cross-repo contract graph from the server when sibling repos are not checked out (`impact` and `contracts` still read local files), and running `verify` on the server against deployed apps (deployed sandbox apps sit behind email sign-in, so it needs a service identity first).

# Traceability and Drift

## Problem & Value
Code changes faster than the documents that describe it. Without a continuous answer to "which spec owns this file, which tests cover this requirement, and has the code moved since the spec was written?", specs rot silently and tests stop meaning anything. Reviewers and auditors cannot tell whether a requirement is implemented, tested or merely written down.

This capability computes that answer on demand and without opinion. It links specs to source files, tests and docs; reports which source files have no owning spec or no test; lists specs that have no code or still have unchecked criteria; checks whether the tests actually exercise each scenario and claim; and detects when source has changed in a way the spec no longer describes. The result is a single, CI-gateable picture of spec health, expressed in stable exit codes and JSON files under `.specguard/`.

## Users & Journeys
- A developer runs `specguard status` before opening a pull request to learn which source files still lack a spec or a test.
- A CI job runs `specguard drift --since main` and fails the build when code changed in ways the spec does not describe.
- An auditor runs `specguard matrix --format csv` to hand compliance a spec-to-test-to-doc traceability table, with per-claim test linkage.
- A tech lead runs `specguard gap-analysis` to see which specs have no implementation yet and gets a build plan per missing spec to hand to a coding agent.
- A QA engineer runs `specguard align` to learn which spec scenarios and claims no test actually exercises.

## Requirements
- [ ] Status reports, for every configured app, how many non-test source files have an owning spec and how many have a test, and lists the files without a spec; test files are never counted as source files that need their own spec. <!-- claim: status-coverage-report -->
- [ ] Status exits with the missing-specs code (4) when any source file lacks a spec and 0 otherwise, never calls the LLM and never writes files; an app with no matching source files is not an error. <!-- claim: status-exit-code -->
- [ ] A spec counts as having a test when a test carries one of its claim tags or a test file matches its name, with the claim tag taking precedence over the file-name fallback. <!-- claim: no-test-by-claim-tag -->
- [ ] When a proof ledger exists status appends a proofs summary, and that summary never changes the exit code. <!-- claim: proof-lines-informational -->
- [ ] All pipelines identify specs by one canonical spec key, so tags, registry entries, matrix rows and alignment entries agree across per-app spec directories. <!-- claim: canonical-keys -->
- [ ] The traceability matrix lists, for every spec, its title and the test files, doc files and source files linked to it, and exits 0 because it is informational. Tests are discovered from the configured test output, test source globs and extra test sources, and the matrix is written as JSON by default or CSV on request, scoped to one app when asked. <!-- claim: matrix-links-all-artifacts -->
- [ ] Each matrix entry lists its claims with the tests whose title, tag or annotation carries that claim's tag, and a test file that carries a claim tag is listed even when its name does not match the spec. <!-- claim: per-claim-linkage -->
- [ ] Gap analysis classifies each spec as unimplemented (no owning source), partial (source exists but unchecked criteria remain) or implemented, ignoring test files when deciding whether source exists. <!-- claim: gap-classification -->
- [ ] Gap analysis writes `.specguard/gaps.json` on every run, writes an agent-readable summary plan when any gap exists, generates LLM implementation plans only for unimplemented specs and never when planning is disabled, and survives an LLM failure without throwing. <!-- claim: gap-artifacts-and-plans -->
- [ ] Gap analysis exits with the missing-specs code (4) when any gap exists and 0 otherwise, and can be restricted to a single spec. <!-- claim: gap-exit-code -->
- [ ] Alignment settles claims and scenarios deterministically from claim tags and scenario names in test titles, and sends only what remains uncovered, with the tests that plausibly relate to it, to the LLM. <!-- claim: align-prepass-first -->
- [ ] Alignment makes no LLM call for a spec with nothing left uncovered, scores deterministic and LLM-covered scenarios together, records covered and uncovered claims per entry, and checkpoints `.specguard/alignment.json` after every spec. <!-- claim: align-score-and-checkpoint -->
- [ ] Drift records a content hash per source file in a portable drift registry keyed by repo-relative POSIX paths, skips the LLM when a file's hash is unchanged, and asks the LLM for a semantic verdict only when it changed. <!-- claim: drift-hash-registry -->
- [ ] On the first run, or with `--mtime`, drift falls back to comparing source and spec modification times, and it still populates the registry; `--force` re-evaluates every file regardless of hash. <!-- claim: drift-mtime-fallback -->
- [ ] Drift exits with the drift code (3) when any spec has drifted, treats a changed source file with no spec as drift, warns and scans all configured sources when git is unavailable, and reports specs with no matching source as orphans. <!-- claim: drift-exit-and-orphans -->
- [ ] A stored proof whose recorded spec hash or drift-registry file hash no longer matches is reported as drift. <!-- claim: stale-proof-is-drift -->
- [ ] For v2 specs a claim's hash covers only that claim's text and the Problem & Value section, so editing other claims, scenarios, frontmatter or history does not make a proof stale, while changing Problem & Value does. <!-- claim: claim-scoped-hash -->
- [ ] one trace model (system, capability, claim) behind a single `check` command whose legacy aliases (`status`, `gap-analysis`, `drift`, `matrix`, `align`) return identical results. <!-- claim: planned-unified-check -->
- [ ] drift is evaluated per capability from all of its source files, reports at claim level, and chunks large diffs so a capability-sized spec stays within the LLM context. <!-- claim: planned-capability-drift -->
- [ ] `check` summary exits 2 on spec rule violations, 4 when a source file has no owning spec or a non-planned capability owns no files, and 0 otherwise; `--coverage`, `--gaps` and `--matrix [--csv]` render the same trace model, which is also written to `.specguard/trace.json` <!-- claim: check-exit-codes -->
- [ ] A v2 proof goes stale for a changed owned file only when no drift assessment covers that exact file version, or the assessment names the claim; a changed file nobody assessed stales every claim of its capability <!-- claim: claim-scoped-file-staleness -->
- [ ] Capability drift baselines a capability on its first run, afterwards assesses only files whose content changed, records an assessment per file version, skips lockfiles and build output without a model call, treats a missing verdict as affecting every claim, and reports changed files no capability owns <!-- claim: capability-drift-assessments -->
- [ ] Large capability diffs are filtered, ranked with interface-like files first, packed into chunks of about 40k characters (an oversized file reduced to headers and declarations), and capped per capability with the remainder reported for manual review <!-- claim: drift-chunking -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: A new file has no spec
**Steps:**
1. A developer adds a source file that no spec lists or matches.
2. They run `specguard status`.

**Expected Results:**
- The report lists the file as missing a spec and the totals show coverage below 100%.
- The command exits with code 4.
- No LLM call is made and no file is written.

### Scenario 2: Source changes in a way the spec does not describe
**Steps:**
1. A registry already exists from an earlier `specguard drift` run.
2. A developer changes an exported function's behaviour in a source file owned by a spec.
3. CI runs `specguard drift --since main`.

**Expected Results:**
- The changed file's hash differs from the registry, so the LLM is asked whether the diff affects the spec.
- When the verdict is drift, the spec is listed, the summary reads `drift: <N> spec(s) drifted` and the exit code is 3.
- Unchanged files are skipped without an LLM call.

### Scenario 3: First drift run on an existing repository
**Steps:**
1. A repository has specs but no `.specguard/drift-registry.json`.
2. The developer runs `specguard drift`.

**Expected Results:**
- A modification-time comparison reports source files newer than their specs.
- The registry is created with a hash per source file so later runs use hashes.
- The command does not fail on a shallow clone or missing git history; it warns and scans all sources.

### Scenario 4: Editing one claim does not stale another claim's proof
**Steps:**
1. A capability spec has claims `a` and `b`, and a proof exists for `b`.
2. A developer rewrites the text of claim `a` and adds a scenario.
3. Status or drift is run.

**Expected Results:**
- The claim hash of `b` is unchanged, so its proof is not stale.
- The claim hash of `a` changed, so any proof of `a` is stale.
- If the Problem & Value section is edited, every claim's hash changes.

### Scenario 5: Auditor exports the traceability matrix
**Steps:**
1. Tests carry `@claim:<specKey>#<claimId>` tags in their titles.
2. The auditor runs `specguard matrix --format csv --out audit/trace.csv`.

**Expected Results:**
- The file lists every spec with its tests, docs and source modules.
- Claim linkage in the JSON form shows which tests carry each claim, including test files whose names do not match the spec.
- The command exits 0 and prints how many entries were written.

### Scenario 6: Alignment only spends tokens on what is uncovered
**Steps:**
1. A spec has three scenarios and two claims. Tests name two scenarios in their titles and tag one claim.
2. The developer runs `specguard align`.

**Expected Results:**
- Only the remaining scenario and claim are placed in the LLM prompt, with tests that relate to the spec.
- A spec whose scenarios and claims are all settled makes no LLM call and scores 100.
- `.specguard/alignment.json` records covered and uncovered claims for the spec.

## Security & Data Considerations
These pipelines read source, specs and tests and write only JSON, CSV and Markdown plans under `.specguard/`. The drift registry stores hashes, timestamps and verdicts, never file content or credentials, and uses repo-relative keys so it can be committed and compared across machines. Hashes detect change; they are not an integrity guarantee against an adversary. Diffs and spec excerpts sent to the LLM for drift and alignment are subject to the configured redaction. LLM keys are referenced by environment variable name only and never appear in plans, `gaps.json` or the registry. Plan file names derive from the spec key with path separators replaced. Traceability output reveals spec and test names, so treat the output directory as internal.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard status`, `specguard gap-analysis [--spec <key>] [--all] [--no-plan]`, `specguard matrix [--out <path>] [--format json|csv] [--app <name>]`, `specguard align [--app] [--spec] [--all] [--concurrency <n>] [--fresh] [--extra-tests <globs...>]`, `specguard drift [--since <ref>] [--spec <key>] [--force] [--mtime]`.
- MCP tools: `specguard_status`, `specguard_drift`, `specguard_matrix`, `specguard_gap_analysis`, `specguard_check`.
- Files under `.specguard/`: `drift-registry.json`, `gaps.json`, `plans/<feature>.md`, `plans/gap-analysis-<timestamp>.md`, `alignment.json`, `traceability.json` (path configurable through `matrix.output`).
- Exit codes: 0 success, 3 drift detected, 4 missing specs or gaps present, 1 internal error.
- `specguard check` with the legacy commands as aliases.

## Out of Scope
- Running tests or recording proof verdicts (see conformance-testing).
- Judging the running system in a browser (see agentic-verification).
- Writing or rewriting specs (see spec-authoring).
- Serving the matrix over HTTP (see documentation-api).

# Workspaces - Multi-Repo and Monorepo

## Problem & Value
Real systems are rarely one repo with one package. A web app calls an API in another repo, a test repo drives both, a docs repo describes them, and a monorepo may hold a dozen packages. A spec checker that sees one repo at a time cannot tell you that changing a provider's interface breaks a consumer elsewhere, and a tool that creates one set of specs per package recreates the file-level granularity problem one level up.

This capability lets several repos, or several packages in one monorepo, be treated as one system. It records which repos take part and what role each plays, detects monorepo packages and their test commands, keeps a graph of the contracts between specs across repos, and answers the question "if this spec changes, what else is affected and what should I re-check?". The planned half unifies repos and packages into a single idea of a unit so that checking, drift, testing, serving and security all work per unit and per capability.

## Users & Journeys
- A platform lead runs `specguard workspace init` in a folder of sibling repos to register them with sensible roles and then reviews the manifest.
- A developer declares in a spec that it depends on another repo's spec, runs `specguard contracts`, and gets the cross-repo graph.
- A provider-API developer runs `specguard impact <spec>` before changing an interface and sees every consumer spec, by depth, with suggested drift commands.
- A release manager runs `specguard workspace drift --since origin/main` to check consumer repos whose providers changed.
- A developer in a pnpm monorepo runs `specguard init` and gets each package's test command recognised.
- An architect runs `check` at a workspace root and sees the system, its units (repos or packages) and the capabilities that span them.

## Requirements
- [ ] A workspace manifest at `.specguard/workspace.json` lists repos with a path and a role of consumer, provider, test or docs, an optional description, and an optional catalog directory; it is found by walking up from any child directory and unknown fields are preserved <!-- claim: workspace-manifest -->
- [ ] A missing manifest is a clear "not found" configuration error and an invalid or schema-failing manifest is a configuration error; repos without their own SpecGuard config load with no config rather than failing <!-- claim: manifest-errors -->
- [ ] `workspace init` registers sibling repos that have a SpecGuard config, deriving each repo key from the directory name alone and each role from the repo's contents (test frameworks, UI or server dependencies, API schema files, language markers) and never from a platform-specific name; it never overwrites an existing manifest and fails with guidance when no repo is found <!-- claim: workspace-init-heuristics -->
- [ ] `workspace status` shows each repo with its role, spec count, incoming and outgoing contract edges and configuration health, plus contract health (verified versus stale edges and a breakdown by edge type), and tells the user to build the graph when none exists <!-- claim: workspace-status -->
- [ ] Monorepo detection reads pnpm, Yarn and npm workspaces, Nx, Turbo and Lerna configuration, expands package globs honouring exclusions, reports the package manager, and records each package's name, directory, test framework and whether it has a test script; a single-package repo is reported as not a monorepo <!-- claim: monorepo-detection -->
- [ ] Each monorepo package gets a test command that runs only that package's tests through the repo's own tooling (Nx, Turbo, pnpm, Yarn or npm), and `init --single` opts out of per-package handling <!-- claim: per-package-test-command -->
- [ ] The contract graph is stored in `.specguard/contracts.json` as nodes (a spec in a repo, identified `<repo>::<specPath>`) and directed edges from consumer to provider with a type of graphql, rest, iframe, upload, event, test or docs, a surface list, a last-verified time and a source <!-- claim: contract-graph-model -->
- [ ] `contracts` builds edges from structured contract blocks in spec Dependencies sections, from importers supplied by enabled plugins and, only with `--with-llm`, from free-text dependencies of specs that have no structured block; lines that do not match the format are skipped <!-- claim: contract-sources -->
- [ ] Building the graph is idempotent and incremental: existing edges are preserved and surface items merged, `--force` rebuilds from scratch, `--repo <key>` restricts to one repo, validation problems such as an edge naming a missing node are warnings that do not fail the command, and the file is written atomically <!-- claim: contracts-idempotent -->
- [ ] `impact` accepts a node id, a workspace-relative path or an absolute path, walks consumers breadth-first to a depth limit (default 6), separates direct from transitive consumers with the connecting edge type and surface, and `--upstream` also lists the providers the target depends on <!-- claim: impact-blast-radius -->
- [ ] `impact` suggests a drift command for each affected consumer repo and an "update docs" suggestion for docs-type edges, reports "no downstream consumers" with exit 0, and exits 1 with an example id format for an unresolvable target or with guidance when no graph exists; it never modifies files <!-- claim: impact-suggestions -->
- [ ] `workspace drift` finds repos with changes since a git ref (default the previous commit), maps changed files to graph nodes, runs drift in the affected consumer repos for the dependent specs, supports `--force` and `--repo`, and exits 3 when any consumer has drifted <!-- claim: workspace-drift -->
- [ ] A claim can be referenced across repos as `repo:specKey#claim` (or `specKey#claim` within the current repo), so a journey or proof can depend on a claim in another repo <!-- claim: cross-repo-claim-refs -->
- [ ] A workspace-level `.specguard/.env` supplies shared keys to every repo in the workspace, with a per-repo `.specguard/.env` taking precedence and real environment variables never overwritten <!-- claim: shared-env -->
- [ ] A workspace is a set of units, where a unit is a repo or a package (`kind: repo|package`) listed under `units` in the manifest and a manifest may mix both; existing `repos` manifests load unchanged as units of kind repo, a repo-kind unit is also visible under `repos`, and a key listed as both is rejected <!-- claim: units -->
- [ ] A claim ref that names a package unit (`web:capabilities/auth#login`) means the workspace root's claim: proofs and test tags carrying it are stored and found under the unprefixed ref, and journey references through a package unit resolve; refs naming a separate repo are left alone. Planned: a capability may also live inside one unit's own spec tree <!-- claim: unit-claim-refs -->
- [ ] Detection also covers Go (`go.work`), Cargo workspaces and uv workspaces besides JavaScript ones, and a repo may hold several; `init` writes one app per ecosystem over every package's sources plus a units manifest carrying each package's test command, instead of one app per package, with glob negations kept at the front <!-- claim: more-ecosystems -->
- [ ] `check` reports each unit's source files, unowned files and the capabilities touching it (a capability spanning packages appears in each, and gets one drift verdict); `test run` runs each package unit's own command, only named units with `--unit`, or with `--affected [--since <ref>]` the changed units plus every unit that depends on them, running everything when a changed file is outside every unit; `serve` exposes the rollup at `/api/v1/units`, and security plan items carry the unit key <!-- claim: unit-aware-pipelines -->
- [ ] Dependencies between units, read from each unit's own manifest (package.json, go.mod, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml), become `package` contract edges with source `workspace`, rebuilt on every `contracts` run so a removed dependency disappears; `impact` accepts a unit or a file inside one, and reports the capabilities with code in the affected units as well as the units themselves <!-- claim: package-edges -->

## Scenarios
### Scenario 1: Register a multi-repo system
**Steps:**
1. A folder contains a web app, an API repo, a browser test repo and a docs repo, each with its own SpecGuard config.
2. The user runs `specguard workspace init`.

**Expected Results:**
- `.specguard/workspace.json` lists four repos with keys from their directory names.
- The web app is a consumer, the API a provider, the test repo a test repo and the docs repo docs, judged from their contents.
- Re-running the command reports that the manifest exists and changes nothing.

### Scenario 2: Build the graph and ask about impact
**Steps:**
1. The web app's spec lists a contracts block pointing to an API spec with a GraphQL surface.
2. The user runs `specguard contracts`, then `specguard impact <api-repo>::specs/mutations/designer.md`.

**Expected Results:**
- `contracts.json` holds an edge from the web app spec to the API spec with the mutation names as its surface.
- Impact lists the web app spec as a direct consumer with the surface items and suggests running drift in the web app repo.
- A node with no consumers prints "No downstream consumers found" and exits 0.

### Scenario 3: Cross-repo drift after a provider change
**Steps:**
1. A provider spec changes on a branch.
2. The user runs `specguard workspace drift --since origin/main`.

**Expected Results:**
- The command finds the changed provider spec, looks up its consumers and runs drift in each consumer repo.
- It reports each consumer as drifted, no drift, skipped or error, and exits 3 if any consumer drifted.

### Scenario 4: Monorepo initialisation
**Steps:**
1. A pnpm repo lists `packages/*`, containing `packages/web` and `packages/api`.
2. The user runs `specguard init`.

**Expected Results:**
- Both packages are detected with their test frameworks, and the test commands use `pnpm --filter <name> test`.
- With `--single`, one app covers the whole repo instead.
- A repo without workspaces is treated as a single package.

### Scenario 5: Unknown target
**Steps:**
1. The user runs `specguard impact unknown/path.md`.

**Expected Results:**
- The output explains that the target cannot be resolved and shows the valid node id format.
- The command exits 1 and no file is changed.

### Scenario 6: One capability across two packages
**Steps:**
1. A capability's sources cover `packages/web/**` and `packages/api/**` in a monorepo.
2. A file in `packages/api` changes and the user runs `test run --affected` and `drift` at the workspace root.

**Expected Results:**
- The change maps to the owning unit and then to the capability, which receives one drift verdict.
- Only the affected units' tests run, and a proof recorded through `api:capabilities/auth#logout` is stored as the root claim.

## Security & Data Considerations
- File reads and git commands are bounded to the repos listed in the manifest; paths are resolved relative to the workspace root and the manifest cannot cause reads outside it by default.
- Monorepo detection only reads configuration files and never runs project code or package scripts.
- The graph and manifest contain repo names, spec paths and API surface names, but no secrets. LLM extraction runs only on explicit request (`--with-llm`) and sends spec text, so it should be avoided for sensitive specs.
- Shared environment files may hold API keys; they are git-ignored by `init`, and real environment variables always win over file values.
- `workspace drift` runs the SpecGuard CLI in sibling repos; only repos named in the manifest are touched.

## Interfaces
- CLI: `specguard workspace init [--name]`, `specguard workspace status`, `specguard workspace drift [--since <ref>] [--force] [--repo <key>]`, `specguard contracts [--force] [--with-llm] [--repo <key>]`, `specguard impact <target> [--max-depth <n>] [--upstream]` (target: a node id, a unit, or a file); `specguard test run [--unit <keys...>] [--affected] [--since <ref>]`; `specguard init` (and `--single`) detects monorepos and writes the units manifest.
- MCP tools: `specguard_contracts`, `specguard_impact`, `specguard_workspace_status`, `specguard_workspace_drift`.
- Files: `.specguard/workspace.json` (name, repos with path, role and description, optional catalog), `.specguard/contracts.json` (version, generatedAt, nodes, edges), workspace-level `.specguard/.env`. `units` map in the manifest (path, kind, role, packageName, ecosystem, test command and framework); `.specguard/trace.json` and `GET /api/v1/units` carry the per-unit rollup.
- Spec syntax: a contracts block in the Dependencies section, delimited by `<!-- contracts:start -->` and `<!-- contracts:end -->`, with lines like `<repoKey>::<specPath> [<type>: <surface>, ...]`; claim refs `repo:specKey#claim`.
- Exit codes: 0 success, 1 missing manifest or unresolvable target, 3 drift detected in a consumer.

## Out of Scope
- Managing git operations, branches or releases across repos.
- Automatically editing consumer code or specs when a provider changes; impact only reports and suggests.
- Replacing a monorepo build tool; SpecGuard calls Nx, Turbo and package managers to run tests but does not orchestrate builds.
- Detecting runtime service dependencies by tracing traffic; edges come from declared blocks, plugin importers, optional LLM extraction and package manifests.
