# Functional specs, master system spec, and the four pillars

## Prompt (verbatim)

I want to look at specguard and how it generates specs. I feel like the specs are very granular and linked very closely to individual code files. I would prefer to have our specs be higher level - functional - where a single spec file links to multiple code files and covers functionality linked to user/business value. There needs to be a high-level master spec that describes the entire system, the problems it solves and the value it creates, then summarizes and links to the functional components that deliver the value.

As an example, AI portal now has 329 specs. This is an informational web portal with a training CMS and a few other features. There should be ~10-15 high level functional specs for this portal. It's fine to fan out the functional specs into backend/frontend or other sub groupings. Specs need to link to tests & docs so the key functionality of specguard is preserved.

I'm also concerned specguard itself has gotten very complicated - there are a lot of features. The philosophy is that code is fluid but specs, and the tests that ensure conformance, are the source of truth. It has the following key functional aspects:
1) create/maintain specs for systems. We should also maintain a history of requirements as the code evolves. E.g. this prompt, and the plans that get generated, should be part of the history of the specguard repo.
2) ensure & run conformance tests that prove the current code delivers against the specs. This includes agentic tests that use tools like playwright and LLM analysis to validate functionality against the problem/value. 
3) generate human and AI readable documentation for the system. This incudes user docs and developer docs as well as spec audits like the traceability matrix. Present these via API such that a viewer can retrieve and format the docs dynamically. E.g. user docs shouldn't be a static generation from the specs but rather generated on the fly from the specs using a fast llm like haiku/luna. 
4) run security scans that can also consider the specs and look for issues that are due to spec-level problems as well as code level. The scans can generate remediation plans which can be managed by other systems to automate remediation.

## Follow-up decisions

- Multi-repo support (contracts, impact, workspace) stays in core and also extends to monorepos.
- Code quality, git commit helpers and the feature catalog become generalized plugins. Nothing references any one customer platform directly.
- Docs consumer is `specguard serve` plus a small web UI.
- Requirement history is captured by hooks plus an explicit `history add` command.
- Scope: the SpecGuard redesign plus the AI Portal migration.

## Plan (approved 2026-10-15)

# SpecGuard 0.2: functional specs, four pillars, AI Portal migration

## Context

SpecGuard's founding principle is that **code is fluid, while specs and the conformance tests that prove them are the source of truth.** The tool has drifted from that principle in two ways.

**1. Specs are file-shaped, not value-shaped.**
- `reverse` writes one spec per source file and derives the spec key from the file path (`src/pipelines/reverse-generate.ts:207-267`, `src/core/language-profiles.ts:432`).
- Drift ties source to specs by file name (`src/pipelines/drift.ts:316-331`). The matrix ties tests and docs to specs by basename (`src/pipelines/matrix.ts:85,103`).
- Nothing records the problem a system solves or the value it creates, so agentic validation can only judge against acceptance-criteria bullets.
- **Result in AI Portal:** 485 spec files.
  - 164 of them describe `node_modules` packages (`zod` alone accounts for 140), because the scan has no default excludes.
  - 31 just mirror test folders.
  - Module paths are wrong (`app/` prefix on `lib/` code), and `specs/db/` is stale since the move to DynamoDB.
  - There are 0 claim anchors and 0 `@claim` tags, so nothing is actually linked to tests.
  - The product is really about 13 capabilities.

**2. The tool has outgrown its pillars.**
- About 27K lines of `src`, 29 commands, 30 MCP tools, and a 7.7K-line VS Code extension.
- Spec health is computed five separate ways (`status`, `gap-analysis`, `drift`, `align`, `matrix`), with `analyze` on top.
- Security runs as three overlapping paths (`security`, `deps`, `remediate`).
- Fix plans come in four incompatible formats.
- Docs are static per-spec LLM rewrites with no API.
- There is no requirement history beyond git.

**Goal.** Rebuild around four pillars, with a hierarchical, functional spec model:
- **P1 Specs and history:** a master SYSTEM spec; about 10–15 capability specs, each linked to many code files, tests and docs; and a requirement history holding prompts, plans and decisions.
- **P2 Conformance:** generated and existing tests plus agentic Playwright/LLM verification, all feeding one proof ledger and judged against requirements *and* problem/value.
- **P3 Docs:** a `specguard serve` HTTP API and a small web UI. User and dev docs are generated on demand by a fast model; traceability and audit views come from the same API.
- **P4 Security:** code-level and spec-level scans producing one published `RemediationPlan` JSON schema that other systems can consume. `remediate` executes those plans.

**Decisions taken:**
- Multi-repo support (contracts, impact, workspace) **stays in core and extends to monorepos**, using one workspace model in which a unit is either a repo or a package (Phase 8).
- quality, git-commit and feature-catalog become **generalized plugins**.
- **Nothing names Practera.**
- The docs consumer is `serve` plus a web UI.
- History is captured through hooks plus an explicit command.
- Scope covers the SpecGuard redesign plus the AI Portal migration.

**Release.** Ship as **0.2.0 (breaking)**, published under the npm `next` dist-tag until AI Portal migrates cleanly. This matters because `action.yml:33` defaults to `version: latest`. The parser keeps reading v1 specs, so repos that haven't migrated keep working.

---

## Phase 0: Record intent (dogfood)

1. Create `specs/history/2026-10-15-functional-specs-and-four-pillars.md` in SpecGuard. It holds this prompt verbatim, this approved plan, and the decisions above. Frontmatter fields: `id`, `date`, `kind: prompt+plan`, `author`, `affects`, `source: claude-code`.
2. Draft `specs/SYSTEM.md` as prose only:
   - the problem: code drifts from intent, and AI-written code makes it worse
   - the users: developers, coding agents, reviewers, auditors, security
   - the value it creates
   - the four pillars and the non-goals
   - a capability list

   Its frontmatter becomes machine-checked in Phase 1.

## Phase 1: Spec model v2 (P1 foundation)

**Format.** YAML frontmatter, parsed with the existing `yaml` dep. **Lists must be block lists, with globs quoted.** Flow lists with `{a,b}` or a leading `*` are a YAML error, so the parser reports a clear message instead.

```yaml
---
id: training-learner-journey          # must equal the file's basename; specKey = id
kind: capability                      # system | capability | component | journey
title: AI Mastery Training — Learner Journey
parent: system                        # capability id for components
value: Employees build practical AI skills through guided, gated lessons.
status: active
sources:
  - "lib/training/**"
  - "app/api/training/{modules,activities,progress}/**"
tests:
  - "test/e2e/lesson-flow.spec.ts"
docs:
  - "docs/training/**"
history:
  - 2026-10-15-functional-specs-and-four-pillars
---
```

**Capability sections:**
- `## Problem & Value` (required)
- `## Users & Journeys`
- `## Requirements` (claims, `- [ ] … <!-- claim: id -->`)
- `## Scenarios`
- `## Security & Data Considerations`
- `## Interfaces`
- `## Out of Scope`
- `## Components`

`kind: journey` keeps its existing World, Actors, Invariants and `verifies:` semantics (`src/core/claims.ts:192-217`). `SYSTEM.md` contains Problem, Users, Value, Capability Map, Architecture Overview and Non-goals.

**Code changes:**
- `src/core/types.ts`: add `SpecKind`. Make `sources`, `tests` and `docs` `string[]`; `sources` is a comma-split string today (`spec-key.ts:76-82`, `types.ts:36`), so update every caller. Add `parent`, `value` and `history`.
- `src/core/spec-parser.ts`: parse frontmatter first and fall back to `parseMetaComment`. Note that `parseMetaComment` (`:36`) grabs the *first* HTML comment, so it must skip the frontmatter case. Map `Acceptance Criteria` to `Requirements`.
- New `src/core/spec-graph.ts`, which loads every spec into a tree and provides:
  - an **id→file index**, used by `locateSpec` in `proof.ts:179-222` in place of path derivation
  - `specsForFile(path)`, which can return several specs or none ("unowned")
  - `ownedFiles(spec)`
  - validation: exactly one SYSTEM, known parents, filename equal to `id`, no duplicate claim ids (make `duplicateClaimIds` at `claims.ts:39` a hard gate), and the capability count at or below `granularity.maxCapabilities`
- `spec-key.ts`: `declaredSources` becomes the single file→spec resolver for every pipeline.
- **Workspace-aware from day one:** every spec graph node carries a `unit` (default: the repo itself), and `specsForFile` takes workspace-relative paths. Monorepo and multi-repo support (Phase 8) then plugs in without reworking the graph.
- **Default excludes** in `config.ts`, always applied: `node_modules`, `dist`, `.next`, `build`, `coverage` and `.git`. The `tests` source group no longer feeds spec generation. Also fix the `featureFromPath` doc/code mismatch.
- **Claim-scoped staleness.** Today any change to the spec or file hash marks every proof stale (`proof-ledger.ts:54-59`). With capability-sized specs that would trip CI constantly, because `proof-stale` is a default fail-on gate (`action/run-gates.mjs:25`). The fix: a proof records the **claim hash**, computed over the claim text plus the normative sections (Problem & Value, Requirements, Interfaces) and leaving out frontmatter such as `history`/`sources`. File staleness comes from claim-level drift verdicts (Phase 4), not from raw file hashes.
- **Model tiers:** add `llm.models: { fast, frontier }`. The pipelines that need them are `summarize`, `docs`, `history` and `spec-review` (`config.ts:83-99`). The defaults are the LiteLLM aliases `fast` and `frontier`.
- **SpecGuard's own migration** (moved here from Phase 0, because it needs this parser):
  - Write 9 capability specs:
    - `spec-authoring`
    - `requirement-history`
    - `traceability-and-drift`
    - `conformance-testing`
    - `agentic-verification`
    - `documentation-api`
    - `security-and-remediation`
    - `workspaces` (multi-repo and monorepo)
    - `integration-surfaces`
  - Move the 104 v1 specs to `specs/_archive/v1/`.
  - Collapse the 6 apps in `.specguard/config.json` into one.
  - This hand migration becomes the golden reference for `consolidate`.

## Phase 2: Generating and migrating specs (P1)

All of this sits under `specguard spec …`. `reverse` and `import` stay as aliases.

**`spec draft`** works as map → cluster → synthesize:
1. **Inventory**, with no LLM: tree, routes, handlers, README/CLAUDE.md, existing specs, tests and docs.
2. **Summarize:** the `fast` model writes a summary per file, cached by content hash in `.specguard/cache/summaries.json`.
3. **Cluster:** the `frontier` model proposes SYSTEM and a capability map (id, value, globs, rationale), bounded by `granularity.target` (default 8–15). It writes `.specguard/spec-map.md` for human review, deliberately outside `plans/` because the extension lists that folder (`host.ts:981`). `--yes` skips the review.
4. **Synthesize** each capability from its file summaries plus key interface files.

This reuses `llmGenerateObject`, `writer.ts`, and the concurrency in `reverse-generate.ts`.

**`spec consolidate`** migrates v1 specs to v2. It clusters existing specs and then merges their requirements. Claim handling is a **one-shot rewrite, not runtime aliasing.** Runtime aliasing can't keep proofs alive, because ledger lookup is exact-key (`proof.ts:434`) and ingest requires the anchor in the located file (`proof.ts:323`).
- **Slug rules:**
  - keep the slug if it is unique within the capability
  - if two bullets have identical text, merge them and map both old refs to the one claim
  - otherwise prefix the old leaf name (`<leaf>-<slug>`, within the 48-character cap)
  - never use encounter-order numeric suffixes (`claims.ts:66-71`)
- **Rewrite** `@claim` tags in tests and journey `verifies:` refs.
- **Rekey** the proof ledger rows (left `stale`, which is honest) and the drift registry.
- **Write `.specguard/claim-migration.json`** as the report. For one release, `results ingest` accepts old refs through this map, so CI results and cross-repo `repo:` refs still carrying old tags keep working.
- **Archive** the v1 specs, and delete specs whose module resolves under excluded paths.
- In AI Portal there are no claims to preserve, so claims are assigned fresh by `spec claims`.

**Other commands:**
- `spec import`: the existing `import.ts`, which now targets a capability and records a history entry.
- `spec claims`: the existing `claims assign/list`.
- `spec index`: regenerates the marked Capability Map region of SYSTEM.md using the `root-doc-sync` markers (`src/core/root-doc-sync.ts`). Prose stays human-owned.

## Phase 3: Traceability model (backbone for P1, P2 and P3)

**Trace model.** New `src/core/trace.ts` builds one model: system → capability → claim, with tests, proof verdict, staleness, docs, last history entry and drift. Inputs:
- the spec graph
- owned files
- `tests:` globs and `@claim` tags (`buildClaimTestIndex`, `claim-tags.ts:118`)
- the proof ledger
- docs globs
- history
- the drift registry

It is written to `.specguard/trace.json`. **Through 0.2.x it also writes the legacy views derived from it:**
- `traceability.json`
- `alignment.json`, which `run-gates.mjs:195` reads
- `analysis.json`, `fix-plan.json`, `gaps.json`, `code-quality.json` and `dep-check.json`, which the extension reads at `host.ts:396,407,454,910-911`

That keeps the extension and the Action working unchanged.

**`specguard check`** replaces `status`, `gap-analysis`, `matrix`, `analyze` and `align`:
- views: `--coverage`, `--gaps`, `--matrix [--csv]`, `--drift`, `--align`
- every old command stays as an alias with **identical args, `--json` shape and exit codes**
- `status` stays indefinitely, because the existing hooks match the substring `specguard status` (`scaffold.ts:291`)

**Capability drift with claim-level output:**
1. Get the git diff (`-U2 --diff-algorithm=histogram`) and map changed files to capabilities with `specsForFile`.
2. Filter out lockfiles, generated files and snapshots. Test diffs are handled separately.
3. Rank the remaining files by interface relevance: routes, handlers, exported-signature changes.
4. Pack them into chunks of about 40k characters. A file over budget is reduced to its hunk headers plus changed exports.
5. Every chunk gets the full Requirements (with claim ids) plus Problem & Value. The output is `{drifted, affectedClaims[], unspecifiedBehaviour[]}`.
6. Merge the chunk results as a union, up to a per-capability chunk cap. Above the cap, report "too large, review manually" with the file list.

`affectedClaims` drives claim-level staleness. `unspecifiedBehaviour` and unowned changed files both show up as spec gaps.

## Phase 4: Requirement history (P1)

**Storage.** New `src/core/history.ts` and `src/pipelines/history.ts`. Entries are committed under `specs/history/YYYY-MM-DD-<slug>.md`.

**Commands:**
- `history add --prompt|--plan <file>|--decision|--affects`: when `--affects` is missing, the `fast` model proposes which capabilities are affected, using the text plus the diff. It also updates the `history:` back-refs in those capabilities. Claim hashes exclude frontmatter, so this does not mark proofs stale.
- `history log [--capability]`: shows the timeline.
- `history inbox`: reads the hook's JSON from stdin, redacts it, and prints nothing.
- `history capture`: also reads stdin.

**Hooks** are opt-in via `init --history-hooks`, and enabled for SpecGuard and AI Portal:
- Generalize `mergeClaudeSettings` (`scaffold.ts:275-319`) from one hardcoded hook to a table of `{event, matcher?, marker, command}`, keeping the idempotent merge and `--update-hooks` rules.
- **`UserPromptSubmit` → `history inbox`:**
  - Stdout is injected into the model's context, so the command must print nothing.
  - It uses the resolved local binary (no `npx` cold start) and ends with `|| true`.
  - It parses real JSON. The current hook uses `sed` (`scaffold.ts:264`), which breaks on quotes and newlines.
  - It appends to `.specguard/history/inbox.jsonl` (uncommitted, size-capped like `activity-hook.ts`), keyed by `session_id` and `cwd`.
- **`PostToolUse` on `ExitPlanMode` → `history capture`:**
  - Reads the plan from `tool_input.plan`, falling back to `transcript_path`.
  - Pairs it with prompts **from the same `session_id`**, so concurrent sessions don't cross-contaminate.
  - Writes one committed entry. Prompts that never lead to a plan are not committed.
  - Verify during implementation that the hook fires only when the plan is approved.
- **Redaction** with `createRedactor(…, 'text')` (`src/core/redact.ts:79`) happens both at inbox write and at capture.

**Reporting.** `check` flags capabilities whose sources changed with neither a history entry nor a spec edit.

## Phase 5: Conformance (P2)

- **`test generate`:** `forward-generate.ts`, now driven by capability Scenarios. Output goes to `<testOutput>/<capability>/…` with `@claim` tags.
- **`test run`:** runs the configured test command and then ingests the results (`results.ts`, test-runner adapters) in one step. `results ingest` and `proof ingest/status` stay as they are, because they are the entry point for CI and external systems.
- **`test heal`:** `heal.ts`, unchanged.
- **`verify`:** `validate.ts`, using the Playwright adapters and guardrails, with three changes:
  1. Goals are built per capability from Users & Journeys and Scenarios, so the agent drives complete journeys.
  2. The judge also receives **Problem & Value**. It returns per-claim verdicts plus a capability-level judgement: does the observed behaviour deliver the stated value? Gaps become findings.
  3. Verdicts are written to the proof ledger through `ingestVerdicts` (`proof.ts:294`) with `evidence: agentic`. Today they live only in `validation-history.json`.

## Phase 6: Documentation API and web UI (P3)

**Server.** `specguard serve [--port 4317]` lives in a new `src/server/`, built on `node:http`. It binds to localhost, has no new framework dependency, and is read-only.

**Endpoints** under `/api/v1`, all derived from the trace model and the spec graph:
- `GET /system`, `/capabilities`, `/capabilities/:id`, `/capabilities/:id/history`, `/history/:id`
- `GET /trace` (the matrix) and `GET /audit` (coverage, stale proofs, drift, gaps, unowned files)
- `GET /docs/:audience/:id` and `/docs/:audience/system`, where the audience is `user`, `dev` or `agent`:
  - Docs are generated **on demand** by `llm.models.fast`. `llm.ts` has no streaming (`:369-394`) and replay doesn't cover streams, so responses are not streamed.
  - Results are cached in `.specguard/cache/docs/` by `(specHash, audience, promptVersion)`, with single-flight so identical concurrent requests produce one LLM call.
  - Budgets are **per request**. The budget in `llm-runtime.ts:26` is process-wide, and a long-running server would exhaust it.
  - The `user` audience leaves out claims and internals, `dev` adds sources, interfaces and tests, and `agent` is a compact structured form.
- `GET /security/plans`, `/security/plans/:id`
- `doc-generate.ts` folds into this shared generator.

**Web UI.** A small static SPA served at `/`, reusing the extension's React webview pieces where they fit (`extension/src/webview/`). Views:
- system overview
- capability detail: value, requirements with proof status, tests, docs and history
- user and dev docs
- matrix and audit
- security plans

**Deferred to a follow-up:**
- the VS Code extension becoming a thin API client. It keeps working through the legacy views in the meantime.
- write endpoints
- OpenAPI
- static `docs build`

## Phase 7: Security and remediation (P4)

**`specguard security scan`** merges `security --with-sast`, `deps` and remediate's detection into one detector set. It reuses:
- `adapters/docker.ts` and the Semgrep call in `security.ts`
- `npm-audit.ts` and `pip-audit.ts`
- `pipelines/remediate/` detection: advisory, ecosystems, gitleaks

**New spec-level review**, using the `spec-review` model per capability. It reads Problem & Value, Users, Requirements, Interfaces, and Security & Data, and flags:
- missing authz or data-classification requirements
- unspecified abuse cases or rate limits
- contradictory requirements
- interfaces with no owning claim
- code findings that reveal a spec gap

Finding types are `spec`, `code`, `dependency` and `secret`.

**`RemediationPlan` schema.** `src/core/remediation-schema.ts` is a Zod schema, also exported as JSON Schema to `schemas/remediation-plan.v1.json`. Each item has:
- finding refs and severity
- capability and claim links
- affected files
- change type: `code`, `spec`, `dependency` or `config`
- verification, meaning the claims that must stay proven

## Phase 8: Workspaces: multi-repo and monorepo, one model

**One model.** A **workspace** is a set of **units**, and a unit is either a separate repo or a package inside a monorepo. `.specguard/workspace.json` (`src/core/workspace.ts`) gains `units: { <key>: { path, kind: repo|package, role } }`. The existing `repos` map is read as units of kind `repo`, so current manifests keep working. A repo can be both: a multi-repo workspace can contain a monorepo, whose packages become nested units.

**Spec hierarchy across units:**
- The workspace-root `specs/SYSTEM.md` describes the whole system.
- A capability can live at the workspace root, for cross-cutting functionality whose `sources` span units (for example `apps/web/**` plus `packages/api/**`). It can also live in a unit's own `specs/` when it is local to that unit.
- A unit may have its own `kind: system` spec for a subsystem, whose `parent` is the workspace SYSTEM.
- Claim refs generalize the existing `repo:specKey#claim` prefix (`claims.ts:140-144`) to `unit:specKey#claim`. Journeys can then verify claims across packages as well as across repos.

**Monorepo detection** moves out of `init` and becomes a shared workspace service:
- Keep the JS detection in `src/core/monorepo.ts` (pnpm, yarn, npm workspaces, Nx, Turbo, Lerna).
- Add uv/Poetry workspaces (`pyproject.toml`), Go `go.work`, and Cargo `[workspace]`, through the language profiles (`src/core/language-profiles.ts`).
- `testCommandFor` gains the matching per-ecosystem commands.
- `init` stops generating one config app per package (`src/pipelines/init.ts:60-73`), which recreated the per-file granularity problem at package level. Instead it writes one config plus a units manifest, and `spec draft` clusters capabilities across packages by function, not by package.

**Pipelines that become unit-aware:**
- **`check` and the trace model:** coverage and gaps roll up per unit and per system. `unowned` is reported per unit.
- **Drift:** changed files map to units and then to capabilities. A capability that spans packages gets one drift verdict.
- **`test run`:** runs only the affected units' tests, using Nx/Turbo filters or per-package commands from `testCommandFor`. It ingests results per unit.
- **`contracts` and `impact`:** edges connect capabilities, not files or repos.

**Commands:** `workspace {init,status,drift}` keeps its names. `workspace init` detects a monorepo, multi-repo siblings, or both.

## Plan

# SpecGuard 0.3: local-first with an optional team server (plus the rest of 0.2)

## Context

SpecGuard 0.2 is built: functional capability specs, four pillars, plugins and the AI Portal migration. It sits as one unpushed commit on each feature branch:
- SpecGuard: `feat/v2-phase-0-history-and-system-spec`
- AI Portal: `specguard/functional-specs`

npm `latest` is still 0.1.2.

Wes asked which parts of SpecGuard should run centrally and which locally. The target: install SpecGuard into Claude Code (hooks plus MCP), Claude Desktop (MCP) and VS Code (extension), use a server when one exists, and fall back to local when it doesn't. He also asked that this plan carry every unfinished item from the 0.2 plan.

**Principle.** There is one engine and two hosts.
- The local CLI is always complete, whether a server exists or not.
- The server shares state, caches and slow or costly work. It is never required.
- Git stays the source of truth for specs and requirement history.
- Every client (MCP, VS Code, web UI) talks to the same `/api/v1/projects/:project/...`, served either by a local `specguard serve` or by the central server.

**Facts that shape the design** (from exploration):

*SpecGuard today*
- `serve` is one repo per process, read-only, unauthenticated and loopback-only (`src/server/index.ts`, `api.ts`).
- There is no storage abstraction: about 239 hard-coded `.specguard` paths.
- `ProofRecord` (`src/core/proof-ledger.ts:16-41`) has no origin or branch, and the claim hash (`src/core/claim-hash.ts`) is unversioned.
- LLM spend and config are process-global (`llm-runtime.ts`). Model calls carry no user metadata. The base URL can only be set through env.
- The summary cache key leaves out the model.
- The VS Code extension reads legacy `.specguard/*.json` files and parses the CLI's text output (`extension/src/dashboard/host.ts`, `sidebar.ts`, `workspace-state.ts`).

*Sandbox (deploykit)*
- No EntraID. Edge identity is deploykit's email sign-in, passed to apps as an `X-Deploykit-Email` header.
- Restricted apps block machine callers, so the API app must be public at the edge and do its own token auth. This mirrors `project-tracker-api`.
- No persistent volumes. Each app gets its own Postgres through `{{DK_DB_URL}}`.
- The app must serve under its path prefix, and the health check is prefix-aware.
- Per-user LiteLLM keys exist (`POST /api/v1/me/litellm-key`), and `http://litellm:4000` is reachable inside the network.
- GitHub-hosted runners and webhooks cannot reach the sandbox. Outbound access to GitHub is unconfirmed (it may need `https_proxy=http://proxy.plymouthrock.com:8080`).

**Decisions (Wes):**
- The server **pulls CI artifacts** from GitHub.
- Auth is **deploykit identity plus server-issued tokens**.
- The extension gets **data through the API while runs stay local**.
- **Ship 0.2 first**: its leftovers become Phase 0.

# SpecGuard

## Problem

Code is now written quickly, often by AI agents, and it changes constantly. Intent does not survive that.
Requirements live in chat transcripts and people's heads, tests drift away from what the system is meant to do,
documentation goes stale, and security reviews look only at code, so flaws that are really missing or wrong
requirements get through.

**Principle: code is fluid. Specs, and the tests that prove the code conforms to them, are the source of truth.**

## Users

- **Developers and coding agents** who need to know what a system is supposed to do before changing it.
- **Reviewers and auditors** who need evidence that the code delivers what was promised.
- **Security and risk teams** who need findings tied to requirements, and fixes that other systems can automate.
- **End users and operators** who need accurate documentation of the system as it is now.

## Value

- Specs describe functionality in terms of the user or business value it delivers, not individual files.
- Every requirement can be traced to code, tests, docs and the history of why it exists.
- Conformance is proven, not assumed: unit, integration and end-to-end tests, plus agentic browser tests that judge
  the running system against its stated problem and value.
- Docs are always current because they are generated from the specs when requested.
- Security review covers spec-level flaws as well as code-level ones, and produces remediation plans in a stable
  format that other systems can act on.

## Pillars

1. **Specs and requirement history.** A master system spec, about 10-15 functional capability specs that each link
   to many code files, tests and docs, and a committed history of the prompts, plans and decisions that shaped them.
   See spec-authoring and requirement-history.
2. **Conformance.** Generate, run and heal tests; keep one proof ledger; verify the running system with agentic
   browser tests judged against requirements and against problem and value. See conformance-testing,
   traceability-and-drift and agentic-verification.
3. **Documentation.** User, developer and agent docs generated on demand from the specs by a fast model and served
   over an API, together with audit views such as the traceability matrix. See documentation-api.
4. **Security.** Code and spec-level scans that produce remediation plans in one published schema. See
   security-and-remediation.

Multi-repo and monorepo workspaces (workspaces) run across all four pillars. integration-surfaces covers how people,
agents and CI drive SpecGuard; platform-foundation is the shared engine underneath.

## Capability Map

<!-- specguard:capability-map:start -->
| Capability | Value | Status | Claims |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Agentic Verification](capabilities/agentic-verification.md) | The running system is judged against what its specs say it is for, by a browser agent that can see and use it safely, so requirements are verified end to end and not only line by line. | active | 21 |
| [Conformance Testing](capabilities/conformance-testing.md) | Teams can prove, claim by claim, that the current code delivers what the specs say, and see immediately when a proof is no longer trustworthy. | active | 26 |
| [Documentation and API](capabilities/documentation-api.md) | Anyone, human or AI, can read accurate documentation of the system as it is now, pitched at their level, generated from the specs on request and delivered over an API. | active | 21 |
| [Integration Surfaces - CLI, Agents, CI, IDE and Plugins](capabilities/integration-surfaces.md) | People, coding agents and other systems can drive SpecGuard from wherever they work (terminal, agent harness, CI or IDE) and extend it without forking it. | active | 23 |
| [Platform Foundation](capabilities/platform-foundation.md) | Every SpecGuard capability runs on one predictable engine for configuration, model access, cost control, redaction, file access and exit codes, so behaviour is consistent, safe and testable. | active | 20 |
| [Requirement History](capabilities/requirement-history.md) | Anyone can see which prompts, approved plans and decisions shaped each capability, so the reason behind a requirement survives the chat session that produced it. | active | 15 |
| [Security Scanning and Remediation](capabilities/security-and-remediation.md) | Security and risk teams find flaws in code, dependencies, secrets and the specs themselves, and get fixes proposed with proof that behaviour was preserved, in a form other systems can automate. | active | 22 |
| [Spec Authoring](capabilities/spec-authoring.md) | Teams get an accurate, machine-checked set of functional specs for their system, created from existing code or documents and kept consistent as it grows. | active | 21 |
| [Local-first operation with an optional team server](capabilities/team-server.md) | SpecGuard works fully on one machine, and when a team server exists it also gives everyone shared proof from CI, shared documents and shared plans, without anyone depending on it. | active | 12 |
| [Traceability and Drift](capabilities/traceability-and-drift.md) | At any moment a team can see how every spec relates to its code, tests, docs and proof, and be told as soon as code and specs stop agreeing. | active | 23 |
| [Workspaces - Multi-Repo and Monorepo](capabilities/workspaces.md) | Teams that split one system across several repos or packages can treat it as one system, so a change in one place shows what else must be re-checked. | active | 19 |
<!-- specguard:capability-map:end -->

## Non-goals

- Replacing the test runner, the issue tracker or the CI system. SpecGuard integrates with them.
- Generating one spec per source file. Specs follow functionality, not file layout.
- Hosting a general documentation site. The docs API is for viewers to render from.

passes the maintainers\' guidance to the clustering model, on a retry too [guidance]

nodes.title: Local-first operation with an optional team server
nodes.value: SpecGuard works fully on one machine, and when a team server exists it also gives everyone shared proof from CI, shared documents and shared plans, without anyone depending on it.

claims.text: `specguard publish` writes one snapshot file holding the spec and history markdown, the trace model, the proof rows, the newest remediation plan and the contract graph, tagged with the project name, repository, branch, commit, origin and engine and hash versions; it never includes source code, working-tree files outside the spec tree, or prompts that were not committed as history, and it redacts credentials from every file; with `--push` or `--server` it also sends the snapshot to the project's team server, and a refusal or an unreachable server fails the command while the file is still written

tests.title: writes a snapshot a server would accept: specs, history, trace, proofs, and no source code [snapshot]
redacts credentials from every file and leaves the v1 archive out [redaction]
names the project from the flag, then config, then the directory [project-name]
rejects paths that leave the spec tree, non-markdown files and bad project names [paths]
rejects malformed, oversized and wrong-version input without throwing [malformed]
sends a large snapshot gzip-encoded, so a proxy with a 1 MB cap lets it through [gzip-push]
accepts a gzip-encoded snapshot, because proxies cap uploads at 1 MB, and refuses an expansion bomb or another encoding [gzip]

claims.text: A snapshot is validated before it is written or accepted: the project name is a safe identifier, every file is a markdown file inside the spec tree (no absolute paths, `..` or backslashes), the trace model has its required shape, an unknown version is refused, and anything over the size limit is refused

The API serves every project under `/api/v1/projects/:project/...`, lists projects at `/api/v1/projects`, and on a server with one project also serves the same routes without the prefix; a server with several projects answers an unprefixed route with a pointer to the prefixed form; besides the existing routes it serves specs with their file (and one spec's markdown), coverage per capability and unit, the document list, the contract graph and unresolved findings, and the web UI works under a path prefix and across projects

tests.title: serves one spec\'s markdown from the snapshot [spec-file]
is served under a path prefix, which only a plain path may be [base-path]
asks the server which projects exist, and uses the prefixed API when there is no default [projects]

claims.text: The API reports `apiVersion`, `engineVersion`, `hashVersion` and whether it accepts writes on `/health` and `/version`, so a client can refuse to mix incompatible data

tests.title: refuses a server that is not SpecGuard or speaks another API version, and flags other hash rules [versions]

claims.text: A registry that is not writable (the local `serve`) answers every write with 405; on a writable one a plan item is changed with `PATCH` by a signed-in maintainer, the change is attributed to them, a stale `If-Match` version is refused with 409 and writes nothing, and a lifecycle violation is refused with 422

tests.title: requires a token for plan changes made through the API, attributing them to its owner, and the CSRF header for browser sessions [writes]

claims.text: A team server keeps its state behind one backend interface (snapshots, plans per project, a document cache per project, tokens, an audit trail and model usage), implemented for files and for Postgres and held to the same contract tests; a project is shown from its newest snapshot on the default branch, else its newest overall; concurrent edits to plans lose nothing, with Postgres using a revision check and retry instead of row locks

tests.title: shows a project from its newest snapshot on the default branch, else its newest overall [snapshots-latest]
lists projects, knows which commits it has, and prunes the oldest [snapshots-housekeeping]
stores plans per project, lists them in order, resolves latest, and ignores a plan that does not validate [plans]
loses no update when many items of one plan change at once, and none when the update throws [plan-updates]
caches by namespace and slot per project, replacing an entry in place [cache]
finds tokens by hash, lets only the owner revoke, and tracks use [tokens]
keeps the audit trail and the model usage in order [audit-usage]
refuses a project name that could leave its directory or break a path [project-names]

claims.text: Every route except `/health` needs a credential: a token (a person's, a project's CI token, or the operator's bootstrap token) or, for browsers, the sandbox's signed-in user header, which reads and mints a person's own tokens but never grants an administrative power; a bad token is refused even when the header is present; a project-scoped credential reaches only its project; nobody mints a token more powerful than their own, admin tokens come only from the admin route; tokens are stored as hashes, shown once, revocable by their owner, and audited; changes made from a browser session need the `X-Requested-With` header

tests.title: serves health to anyone and everything else only to a valid credential [auth-gate]
is mounted under its base path and nowhere else [base-path]
refuses a request target that is not a valid path, and an oversized body [bad-input]
lets a signed-in user mint their own token, never more power than they hold, and revoke it [own-tokens]
reserves administration for an admin token: the header never grants it, and the bootstrap token does [admin]
records who made and revoked tokens in the audit log [audit]

claims.text: A project's CI token or a maintainer publishes a snapshot over HTTP, creating the project on first publish; the snapshot's plan is merged with the stored one, so statuses and tracker references that people set on the server survive a republish, an item marked fixed that a scan sees again reopens, and unresolved items the new plan lacks are kept unless that plan was made from the stored one

tests.title: accepts a snapshot from a project\'s CI token and serves the project from it [publish-and-read]
keeps a credential to its own project, and refuses viewers, bad snapshots and a mismatched name [publish-guards]
keeps what trackers changed when CI publishes a newer plan [plan-survives-republish]

claims.text: Documents on a team server are generated once per spec content, audience, prompt version and model and shared by everyone, and each generation runs in its own model scope with the requester's name, the project and the gateway's labels, so spend is attributed to the person who asked and recorded per user and project

tests.title: generates a document once for everyone, and attributes the model spend to whoever asked [docs-shared-and-attributed]

claims.text: The server fetches the `specguard-evidence` artifacts CI uploaded for each configured repository on a timer, publishes the snapshot inside under the configured project with the commit and branch taken from the workflow run, skips what it already has and artifacts that are expired, oversized, invalid or from forks, and reports one repository's failure without stopping the others

tests.title: publishes each new artifact under the configured project, with commit and branch from the run [publish]
does not fetch what it already has, and skips expired, forked, oversized and broken artifacts [skips]
reports a GitHub error for one repository and carries on with the next [error-isolation]
finds the snapshot wherever the upload put the archive root [zip-layouts]

claims.text: The server answers MCP over HTTP at `/mcp` for token holders only, as read-only tools (projects, system, capability, spec, audit, coverage, docs, history, findings, plans) that go through the same API as the same identity, so access rules, project scoping and redaction are the API's

tests.title: needs a token, lists read-only tools, and answers them through the API as the caller [mcp]
keeps a project-scoped token to its project even through MCP [mcp-scope]

claims.text: Commands that can use a server resolve it from config or the environment, check its health with a short timeout and a compatible API version, and otherwise behave locally: reads fall back silently and say which source they used; a shared write goes to the server or, with none, is written locally and marked local-only; a server that answers but refuses (bad token, no permission, lifecycle violation) is an error and never a quiet switch to local; `server.mode: required` makes an unreachable server an error and `off` never contacts it; `check --team`, the plan commands, the MCP plan tool and the VS Code extension all follow this, and a token saved by `login` is checked against the server before it is kept

tests.title: serves the workspace locally when no server is configured [no-server]
uses the team server when it is configured, healthy and has the project, with the token it was given [server]
falls back to the local server, with a reason, when the server is down, refuses, lacks the project or is another version [fallbacks]
never contacts a server when the mode is off, and lets the editor setting win over the project\'s [off-and-override]
reads the project\'s server block, names the project after the directory by default, and finds a token in order [resolve]
reports a command line that does not exist, and one that exits at once, instead of hanging [failures]
gives up when the server never says where it is listening [silent]
saves a token readable by its owner only, per server, and forgets it [save]
comes from config or the environment, takes the token from env or a saved login, and is absent when off [target]
connects to a healthy server, and returns null with the reason when there is none, in auto mode [auto]
treats an unusable server as an error only in required mode [required]
answers a slow server within the timeout by giving up on it [timeout]
sends the snapshot to the server and the project appears there [push]
fails, and says why, when the token is wrong, the server is down, or no server is configured [push-failures]
reads plans from the server when it answers, and from local files, saying so, when it does not [read-fallback]
reads locally, without trying a server, when none is configured [no-server]
writes to the server when it answers, and leaves the local plan alone [write-server]
writes locally and says it is local-only when the server does not answer [write-local]
does not hide a refusal by writing locally: a wrong token is an error and nothing changes [no-silent-switch]
writes locally when the plan has not been published yet, and reports a lifecycle violation instead of working around it [not-on-server]
shows CI\'s proofs set against this working tree\'s [lines]
says no server answered rather than failing [degraded]

nodes.title: Traceability and Drift
nodes.value: At any moment a team can see how every spec relates to its code, tests, docs and proof, and be told as soon as code and specs stop agreeing.

claims.text: Status reports, for every configured app, how many non-test source files have an owning spec and how many have a test, and lists the files without a spec; test files are never counted as source files that need their own spec.

tests.title: scenario 3: reports test coverage
scenario 4: excludes the tests group from the needs-a-spec set

claims.text: Status exits with the missing-specs code (4) when any source file lacks a spec and 0 otherwise, never calls the LLM and never writes files; an app with no matching source files is not an error.

tests.title: scenario 1: exit 0 when all source files have specs
scenario 2: exit 4 when a spec is missing
scenario 5: empty repo reports zero and exit 0

claims.text: A spec counts as having a test when a test carries one of its claim tags or a test file matches its name, with the claim tag taking precedence over the file-name fallback.

tests.title: finds matching test file by basename convention
links claims to tests by tag, honours sources.tests and extraTestSources, and reads result files
status does not report specs with tagged tests as (no test)

claims.text: When a proof ledger exists status appends a proofs summary, and that summary never changes the exit code.
All pipelines identify specs by one canonical spec key, so tags, registry entries, matrix rows and alignment entries agree across per-app spec directories.

tests.title: matrix reports claim-level coverage under canonical keys
migrates old registry keys (api/api/..., api/...) to the canonical key

claims.text: The traceability matrix lists, for every spec, its title and the test files, doc files and source files linked to it, and exits 0 because it is informational. Tests are discovered from the configured test output, test source globs and extra test sources, and the matrix is written as JSON by default or CSV on request, scoped to one app when asked.

tests.title: writes the matrix as JSON or CSV with one row per claim [matrix]
scenario 1: builds matrix for all apps
scenario 2: csv format output
scenario 3: spec with no matching test has tests: []
--app scopes to single app
matrix reports claim-level coverage under canonical keys

claims.text: Each matrix entry lists its claims with the tests whose title, tag or annotation carries that claim's tag, and a test file that carries a claim tag is listed even when its name does not match the spec.

tests.title: links claims to tests by tag, honours sources.tests and extraTestSources, and reads result files
matrix reports claim-level coverage under canonical keys

claims.text: Gap analysis classifies each spec as unimplemented (no owning source), partial (source exists but unchecked criteria remain) or implemented, ignoring test files when deciding whether source exists.

tests.title: gaps lists untested claims and non-proven claims [gaps]

claims.text: Gap analysis writes `.specguard/gaps.json` on every run, writes an agent-readable summary plan when any gap exists, generates LLM implementation plans only for unimplemented specs and never when planning is disabled, and survives an LLM failure without throwing.
Gap analysis exits with the missing-specs code (4) when any gap exists and 0 otherwise, and can be restricted to a single spec.

Alignment settles claims and scenarios deterministically from claim tags and scenario names in test titles, and sends only what remains uncovered, with the tests that plausibly relate to it, to the LLM.

tests.title: collects the union of testOutput, sources.tests, extraTestSources and extra globs
settles claims by tag (with or without repo prefix) and scenarios by title
makes no LLM call when claim tags and scenario titles settle everything
sends only uncovered items and only related test files to the LLM
align covers claims from tags without an LLM call

claims.text: Alignment makes no LLM call for a spec with nothing left uncovered, scores deterministic and LLM-covered scenarios together, records covered and uncovered claims per entry, and checkpoints `.specguard/alignment.json` after every spec.

tests.title: writes alignment.json after a finished run and skips cached specs on the next run
keeps finished specs when one LLM call fails, and retries only the failure
makes no LLM call when claim tags and scenario titles settle everything

claims.text: Drift records a content hash per source file in a portable drift registry keyed by repo-relative POSIX paths, skips the LLM when a file's hash is unchanged, and asks the LLM for a semantic verdict only when it changed.

tests.title: round-trips repo-relative POSIX keys
migrates absolute keys once and does not rewrite a relative registry
updateFileEntry keys by the given key
ingest records source hashes from declared sources (root- and app-relative)

claims.text: On the first run, or with `--mtime`, drift falls back to comparing source and spec modification times, and it still populates the registry; `--force` re-evaluates every file regardless of hash.

tests.title: flags drift when the source is newer than its spec (exit 3)
reports no drift when the spec is newer than the source (exit 0)

claims.text: Drift exits with the drift code (3) when any spec has drifted, treats a changed source file with no spec as drift, warns and scans all configured sources when git is unavailable, and reports specs with no matching source as orphans.

tests.title: surfaces unspecified behaviour and changes to files no capability owns [gaps-from-drift]
flags drift when the source is newer than its spec (exit 3)
flags drift when a changed source has no spec at all (exit 3)
falls back to scanning all sources when git fails (no throw)

claims.text: A stored proof whose recorded spec hash or drift-registry file hash no longer matches is reported as drift.

tests.title: a v1 proof still goes stale on any whole-file change [verdict-v1-unchanged]

claims.text: For v2 specs a claim's hash covers only that claim's text and the Problem & Value section, so editing other claims, scenarios, frontmatter or history does not make a proof stale, while changing Problem & Value does.

tests.title: ignores frontmatter, other claims and scenarios [claim-hash-stable]
changes when the claim text or the Problem & Value changes [claim-hash-sensitive]
changes when only the continuation line of a claim changes

claims.text: one trace model (system, capability, claim) behind a single `check` command whose legacy aliases (`status`, `gap-analysis`, `drift`, `matrix`, `align`) return identical results.

tests.title: status, gap-analysis and matrix delegate with their own names and exit codes [aliases]

claims.text: drift is evaluated per capability from all of its source files, reports at claim level, and chunks large diffs so a capability-sized spec stays within the LLM context.

tests.title: stales only the claims the change affects, one model call for the capability [claim-level]

claims.text: `check` summary exits 2 on spec rule violations, 4 when a source file has no owning spec or a non-planned capability owns no files, and 0 otherwise; `--coverage`, `--gaps` and `--matrix [--csv]` render the same trace model, which is also written to `.specguard/trace.json`

tests.title: summary reports ownership, tests and proofs, exits 4 for unowned files [summary]
exits 0 once every source file has an owner [clean-exit]
exits 2 and names the rule on a graph error [graph-error]
counts each graph error once in the failed total [failed-count]

claims.text: A v2 proof goes stale for a changed owned file only when no drift assessment covers that exact file version, or the assessment names the claim; a changed file nobody assessed stales every claim of its capability

tests.title: a v2 proof stays proven when only the whole-file hash moved [verdict-claim-scoped]
without a drift run, a changed owned file stales every claim of the capability [unassessed]
a later "unaffected" assessment does not clear an earlier "affects this claim" one [assessment-chain]
a source edit stales exactly the claims of the specs that declare it

claims.text: Capability drift baselines a capability on its first run, afterwards assesses only files whose content changed, records an assessment per file version, skips lockfiles and build output without a model call, treats a missing verdict as affecting every claim, and reports changed files no capability owns

tests.title: without a drift run, a changed owned file stales every claim of the capability [unassessed]
stales only the claims the change affects, one model call for the capability [claim-level]
keeps proofs when the change affects no requirement [unaffected]
assumes every claim is affected when no verdict can be obtained [no-verdict]
is idempotent: a second run with no new changes makes no model calls [idempotent]
ignores claim ids the model invented and treats the change as affecting every claim [invented-ids]
accepts a claim named as spec#id and keeps the others proven [ref-form-ids]
sends changes under src/build/ to the model, because only top-level build output is skipped [real-source-build-dir]
skips lockfile-style files without a model call [ignored-files]

claims.text: Large capability diffs are filtered, ranked with interface-like files first, packed into chunks of about 40k characters (an oversized file reduced to headers and declarations), and capped per capability with the remainder reported for manual review

tests.title: reduces an oversized diff to headers and declarations [reduce-diff]
packs files into budgeted chunks, interface files first, and reports overflow [pack]

nodes.title: Workspaces - Multi-Repo and Monorepo
nodes.value: Teams that split one system across several repos or packages can treat it as one system, so a change in one place shows what else must be re-checked.

claims.text: A workspace manifest at `.specguard/workspace.json` lists repos with a path and a role of consumer, provider, test or docs, an optional description, and an optional catalog directory; it is found by walking up from any child directory and unknown fields are preserved

A missing manifest is a clear "not found" configuration error and an invalid or schema-failing manifest is a configuration error; repos without their own SpecGuard config load with no config rather than failing

`workspace init` registers sibling repos that have a SpecGuard config, deriving each repo key from the directory name alone and each role from the repo's contents (test frameworks, UI or server dependencies, API schema files, language markers) and never from a platform-specific name; it never overwrites an existing manifest and fails with guidance when no repo is found

tests.title: derives repo keys from the directory name only
classifies by content, not by name

claims.text: `workspace status` shows each repo with its role, spec count, incoming and outgoing contract edges and configuration health, plus contract health (verified versus stale edges and a breakdown by edge type), and tells the user to build the graph when none exists

Monorepo detection reads pnpm, Yarn and npm workspaces, Nx, Turbo and Lerna configuration, expands package globs honouring exclusions, reports the package manager, and records each package's name, directory, test framework and whether it has a test script; a single-package repo is reported as not a monorepo

tests.title: reads pnpm workspaces with exclusions and infers frameworks
reads Yarn and npm workspaces (array and object forms)
detects Nx and Turbo and prefers their runners
returns null for a single package

claims.text: Each monorepo package gets a test command that runs only that package's tests through the repo's own tooling (Nx, Turbo, pnpm, Yarn or npm), and `init --single` opts out of per-package handling

tests.title: writes one app over every package and a units manifest with each package\'s test command [one-config-units]
--single keeps one app and writes no manifest [single]

claims.text: The contract graph is stored in `.specguard/contracts.json` as nodes (a spec in a repo, identified `<repo>::<specPath>`) and directed edges from consumer to provider with a type of graphql, rest, iframe, upload, event, test or docs, a surface list, a last-verified time and a source

`contracts` builds edges from structured contract blocks in spec Dependencies sections, from importers supplied by enabled plugins and, only with `--with-llm`, from free-text dependencies of specs that have no structured block; lines that do not match the format are skipped

Building the graph is idempotent and incremental: existing edges are preserved and surface items merged, `--force` rebuilds from scratch, `--repo <key>` restricts to one repo, validation problems such as an edge naming a missing node are warnings that do not fail the command, and the file is written atomically

`impact` accepts a node id, a workspace-relative path or an absolute path, walks consumers breadth-first to a depth limit (default 6), separates direct from transitive consumers with the connecting edge type and surface, and `--upstream` also lists the providers the target depends on

`impact` suggests a drift command for each affected consumer repo and an "update docs" suggestion for docs-type edges, reports "no downstream consumers" with exit 0, and exits 1 with an example id format for an unresolvable target or with guidance when no graph exists; it never modifies files

`workspace drift` finds repos with changes since a git ref (default the previous commit), maps changed files to graph nodes, runs drift in the affected consumer repos for the dependent specs, supports `--force` and `--repo`, and exits 3 when any consumer has drifted
A claim can be referenced across repos as `repo:specKey#claim` (or `specKey#claim` within the current repo), so a journey or proof can depend on a claim in another repo

tests.title: accepts a repo-qualified ref and a bare ref, and rejects a string with no hash

claims.text: A workspace-level `.specguard/.env` supplies shared keys to every repo in the workspace, with a per-repo `.specguard/.env` taking precedence and real environment variables never overwritten

tests.title: applies the real environment first, then the repo file, then the workspace file [precedence]
does nothing without any env file, and ignores malformed lines [none]

claims.text: A workspace is a set of units, where a unit is a repo or a package (`kind: repo|package`) listed under `units` in the manifest and a manifest may mix both; existing `repos` manifests load unchanged as units of kind repo, a repo-kind unit is also visible under `repos`, and a key listed as both is rejected

tests.title: loads a legacy repos-only manifest as units of kind repo [legacy-repos]
loads a units-only manifest, and a repo-kind unit also appears under repos [units-only]
rejects a key listed as both a repo and a unit [duplicate-key]
finds the owning unit by the deepest matching path [unit-of-file]

claims.text: A claim ref that names a package unit (`web:capabilities/auth#login`) means the workspace root's claim: proofs and test tags carrying it are stored and found under the unprefixed ref, and journey references through a package unit resolve; refs naming a separate repo are left alone. Planned: a capability may also live inside one unit's own spec tree

tests.title: stores a proof for web:capabilities/auth#login under the root claim, so check can see it [unit-ref-proof]
treats a test tag that names a package unit as the root claim [unit-ref-tag]
